ACME workbook

Agents 101

Eight modules. The chat-to-systems leap. Build real agents on your own company content.

Welcome to Agents 101

Want to see what Claude can make? Start with a file you’ll recognize as soon as you see it. Snake needs one message and none of your work files. Later you’ll make a briefing for your working week.

First steps

Using Claude Code or another tool? Switch the handbook to it

1 Ask Claude to make a game

Leave this handbook open. Open Claude Desktop and click New. If you see a Chat/Cowork switch, choose Cowork. Type this into the message box and press Send.

Type in Claude Desktop
Make me a Snake game and link to the file here.

In Claude’s reply Look under your message. The link to the Snake game is the file Claude made for you. Sometimes Claude opens the game board beside the reply as well. If you only get a description, ask “Can you attach the game?”

Once you see the game, come back to this tab and choose Keep my game to save it to your computer.

Make a folder for your game, then send the request below in a session using that folder.

Build me a snake game as a single HTML file. Save it as `prework/snake.html`.

2 Keep my game

Right now your game is in the conversation. Give it a home on your computer so you can open it again. The folder will hold the work you do here, including your calendar briefing.

Your computer
Windows folder walkthrough

Video coming here. The steps below show how to choose the folder.

  1. In File Explorer, open Documents. Click New, then Folder. Name it agents-101.
  2. In your game conversation, click + below the message box, then Add folder.
  3. Below the message box, click Project or folder, then Add folder. You can also find Add folder under +.
  4. In the picker, click Documents in the sidebar, then New Folder. Name it agents-101 and click Create, then Open. If you have the folder already, select it and click Open.
  5. In the picker, open Documents, select agents-101, and confirm your selection.

If Claude asks for permission, click Allow after checking that it names agents-101. When you see agents-101 attached to your message, copy and send this in the same conversation.

5 See what makes this an agent

Your game and your meeting summary were agent work. The agent took your request, used tools and saved files in your folder. What is an Agent names the five parts behind that in its short version.

Contents

  1. 01Getting GoingContext is how you paint by LLM. What you give the agent shapes what comes back, and you can go very deep with it: your profile, your rules, your judgement on the result.→
  2. 02Building Agent SystemsA system remembers, grows, and compounds around the one thing you need to make progress on. Chat can't.→
  3. 03Multi-Agent SystemsSeveral agents can work on one problem together. Split the work, run the agents in parallel, and let them hand off through shared files. Three agents search, three more decide. Handoffs are where work gets lost, so check them.→
  4. 04SecurityYou can't tell if your agent is safe from its output. Run a check; don't wait for certainty.→
  5. 05Grounded OutputThere is truth out there, and your agent's job is to stay connected to it. Where it cannot reach a source, it fills the gap: confident, plausible, wrong. Grounding, and checks you test on your own output, make the gap visible.→
  6. 06EvaluationsPut the Module 5 judge in a loop and the work improves by itself. The generator sharpens against the judge's feedback, round after round, while you walk away.→
  7. 07From Personal to TeamYou can't really share an agent. You can share the context, a skill, the output, or an interface, and choosing between them is a strategy decision.→
  8. 08Agents Building Agents (The Flywheel)Agents building agents is how you and your organisation learn faster. Your agent can improve your agent, and from there a hundred agents is a matter of describing them.→

Getting Going

Big Idea

Context is how you paint by LLM. What you give the agent shapes what comes back, and you can go very deep with it: your profile, your rules, your judgement on the result.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Engineer context
  • Write rules for an agent
  • Judge agent output

Start here

Outputs go in module-1/.

The question, to you: where did LLM output on your work come out generic, and what made it yours?

Lecture

Context is King

Ten versions, no spec

I approach almost all my work with agents now: broad analysis, a first version early, and far more text than I read line by line. Ten iterations is fine.

This autumn three colleagues started building an agent factory. I asked which capabilities they were building. They said they had a few problems to solve.

A colleague has a name for how I work: steering without reading all the text. For a while I felt I had lost a common language with people who write the spec first and meet to agree on it. Their meetings are how they iterate. Mine happen with the agent.

Antti Tevanlinna

What makes the difference?

The same question. Two answers. What makes the difference?

Same question, two answers

In one session, you ask "What is the capital of Italy?" Rome. "What should we have for dinner?" Italian: pasta, osso buco, risotto.

In the other, "What is the largest lake in Finland?" Saimaa. Same dinner question.

Finnish: salmon, rye bread.

The first exchange became context.

It reads the whole conversation every time

The LLM reads the whole conversation every time and generates the next response from all of it. Your first prompt and its answer are part of the input to the second prompt. Change the front, change the back.

That is context. You steer your agent with context.

Context is whatever you tell it

One more window. First prompt: "I'm a cardiologist preparing dinner for my patients." Then the same dinner prompt.

The suggestion shifts: heart-healthy, low-sodium, vegetable-forward. You told the LLM who you are.

Context is whatever you tell it: a fact, a role, a preference.

The first piece of the picture

Context is the first piece of the agent. Tools, goals, checks, boundaries and loops come later and run on it.

A file it reads every time

So far, the context was one message you typed, gone when the session closes.

You can put the context in a file the agent reads at the start of every session. You write it once, and it shapes every answer.

That's a guardrail. That's your turn.

Phase 2: Apply a framework you know

8 min

The site isn't there to sell. A colleague who visits it should think "this is the person I want to work with more, on the things they're great at."

Name the framework and tune it

StoryBrand fits "what kind of help is this person to others." The hero is the colleague, not you. Skip the sales-funnel beats (Stakes, Call-to-Action).

Name the framework, tune it, have the agent run it. The LLM knows StoryBrand, so skip listing its questions. Same for Toyota Kata or SWOT: "Apply X to Y, but tune for Z."

Keep yourself the protagonist, then run the beats

Applied to the whole site, StoryBrand makes the colleague the protagonist. The site stays a personal site; you stay the protagonist of the page. Your name goes in the headline and your current work front and centre. StoryBrand shapes only the colleague-help section.

Prompt (Cowork)

Apply Donald Miller's StoryBrand framework to the COLLEAGUE-HELP SECTION of my personal site, but tuned for ONE goal: when a colleague reads it, they think "this is the person I want to work with more, on the things they're great at." Not buying a service. Not booking a call. A colleague relationship.

Important: this is a PERSONAL site. The protagonist of the SITE is me — my name, my identity, my actual work. The headline is about me, not a question to the visitor. The StoryBrand tune shapes how I describe the help relationship; it does NOT restructure the whole site to make the colleague the hero of the page.

Use these StoryBrand beats for the help section: Character (the colleague — hero of the help relationship, not of the site), Problem (what work they're stuck on or want more of, that I see clearly), Guide (what makes me their natural ally), Plan (what working with me actually feels like — low-friction, informal is fine), Success (what it looks like a year later when we've worked together more — what we shipped, what changed for them).

Skip Stakes and Call-to-Action — no fear-framing, no "book a chat." The site's vibe is the CTA.

Walk me through the five beats. Ask one beat, wait for my answer, then ask the next. Do not show me the remaining beats. Take whatever shape of answer I give. After the fifth answer, regenerate `module-1/site.html` — keep my name and identity at the top, keep my current work front and centre, apply the tuned StoryBrand to the help section. Reshape how the help section sounds, not as a new bullet list — in the voice. Keep the edge in my answers; don't soften.

Phase 4: Anti-branding, the mirror

8 min

Most people can list what drives them mad at work in thirty seconds, but stall on what they're great at. Invert the easy thing. Define what you're for by inverting what you're against. Adam Grant calls a version of this the energy audit; Taleb calls it via negativa.

Name the framework, tune it, ask the agent to run it.

List what you hate, then invert it

List a few specific things you hate about work. Name actual things ("meetings where nobody disagrees," "decks where every page says 'iterating'"), not categories ("bureaucracy"). Vague input drifts back to the statistical-default you.

Prompt (Cowork)

Apply anti-branding (Adam Grant's energy audit version) to my personal site. I'll paste a list of things I hate about work right after this. For each:
1. Take the hate.
2. Associate it with the offerings / colleague-types it implies (what kind of work, what kind of people produce this).
3. Be the opposite — but always speak in the positive. Don't lead with "I don't do X"; lead with what I do instead.
4. Turn blockers / slowness / gaps into progress and outcomes — what I move toward, not what I push away from.

After step 4, regenerate `module-1/site.html`. Use the anti-branding as VOICE — sharpen the headline, the hero line, the section framings, the overall stance. Not as a new "What I'm against" section. The site should sound like someone with a spine wrote it. Keep the edge; don't soften.

Then take maximum freedom on presentation: rethink the page so a colleague lands on it and instantly wants to spend more time with you. You decide structure, ordering, sections, visual rhythm — whatever makes the page actually land. Keep the substance (StoryBrand-tuned help, strengths shaping the voice, anti-branding edge); free hand on the rest.

Phase 5: Look back

6 min

Run this one. The debrief starts from the file it writes, and the agent waits for one answer from you.

Prompt (Cowork)

Look at the very first site you generated from just my LinkedIn profile, before I added any differentiation context. Find three specific claims you made in that version that turned out to be generic, empty, or wrong about me once we added real context. Name them and say why each one was a statistical default rather than something true of me.

Then pick three lines from the current site that are most specifically me. For each, name the piece of context that produced it: my LinkedIn, the colleague-guide frame, my strengths, the mirror-list, or a call I made on a draft. Write both lists to `module-1/context-trace.md`. Before you save, ask me what I gave you that changed the page most, wait for my answer, and write it in my words as the last line.

Phase 6: Free iteration

6 min

Make it yours: color, layout, tone, a quote at the top, a section most sites lack. Iterate until you say "yes, this is me." You drive; no set prompts.

Tip: steal a look and feel by naming a site. The LLM knows famous sites' design by name. Try "Restyle module-1/site.html to feel like X" with two or three sites, such as Stripe, Linear or Patagonia, and keep your favorite.

Phase 7: Close, package what you learned

4 min

Capture the move so a fresh agent can repeat it on someone else's bio.

Prompt (Cowork)

Write a generation rules file at `module-1/personal-brand-generation.md` — a portable agent guideline I could invoke on the next personal-brand task (a colleague's bio, a team page, a client one-pager). Structure it: what this is for, the core rule (distinctive not descriptive), what never to generate, what always to do, the framework moves to apply (StoryBrand-tuned for the help section, anti-branding for voice, visual-steal for chrome), voice rules. Pull from what we just did — the actual decisions, the actual flips, the actual chrome — not from generic guidance. Keep the edge — distinctive over diplomatic. No CTA theatre.

When you're done, summarize in 4–6 lines what's in the file: the structure you used, the strongest 2–3 rules, and anything you weren't sure about. Then tell me to open `module-1/personal-brand-generation.md` and inspect the first two or three rules before I accept it.

See the mechanism repeat in every phase

What happened:

The agent reads everything in the session: your LinkedIn, the colleague-guide frame, strengths, the mirror-list and the site it wrote last. The more specific the context, the more the output is yours.

Take the context move past this site

The point:

The LLM didn't get better between Phase 1 and Phase 6. The context did. The same mechanism scales to business proposals, competitor analysis and product strategy.

This was Recipe 1. When the next output needs the same move, the Cookbook for Agent System Design holds the moves and components.

Lecture

Iterate and Learn

Context became something you can point at

Context is the bit you added that turned a generic About page into a site your neighbour recognised as yours.

What to package: what context the agent needs, what generic looks like, what a stronger pass does differently, and which rule should survive into the next session.

Why the look-back was kind to you

The agent's picks of three generic claims in its own site came back gentle.

Grading its own work is another chance to be helpful: the self-report is the same kind of output as the thing reported on.

The report is a hypothesis, not a result

Read what comes back as a claim about the work, not a verdict on it.

Where the account matches the session as you remember it, two reads agree. Where it doesn't, yours counts.

The agent generated, you decided

Your own knowledge of the subject stood between the generic draft and the page, which is why the site reads as yours. Only you could catch a wrong line about you, so start with your own profile.

You act on the future to know what's real

You act on the future to know what's real. Nobody knows where agents are going, not Anthropic, not your board. The people who figure it out first run the experiment.

Mental models only come from doing.

Five minutes with the agent: the debrief.

Debrief

Five minutes. The retro is a second pass on module-1/personal-brand-generation.md: the agent reads the file against the session and module-1/context-trace.md for what worked, what fell flat, what to keep, what to drop.

Ask the agent to retro your rules file.

Prompt (Cowork)

Start by reading the file. No plan or preamble.

Read `module-1/personal-brand-generation.md` and `module-1/context-trace.md`. Then re-read what we did building the site. Run a retro: which moves landed, which fell flat, where context broke through, where the output stayed generic. Compare the rules file to the actual work. Sort each rule into keep, sharpen, or drop. What's missing the rules should have caught? Find what's still surface; don't defend the file as-is.

Assume the rules file is at least 30% wrong or thin. Find that 30%. If fewer than two rules get dropped or substantially rewritten, say why before you proceed.

Then overwrite `module-1/personal-brand-generation.md` with the retro applied. Sharpen what's weak. Add what's missing. Drop what's wrong. Rewrite the file in place; don't append a "retro notes" section.

When you're done, list:
- dropped: rule text + reason
- sharpened: before -> after
- added: rule text + why the session needed it
- still uncertain: anything the rules should cover but you want me to weigh in on first

Assume the rules file is at least 30% wrong or thin. Find that 30%. If fewer than two rules get dropped or substantially rewritten, say why before you proceed.

Then overwrite `module-1/personal-brand-generation.md` with the retro applied. Sharpen what's weak. Add what's missing. Drop what's wrong. Rewrite the file in place; don't append a "retro notes" section.

When you're done, list:
- dropped: rule text + reason
- sharpened: before -> after
- added: rule text + why the session needed it
- still uncertain: anything the rules should cover but you want me to weigh in on first

The agent updates the file and summarises the changes. Expect the generation rules to change a lot.

Push back on what the retro missed

The LLM is generous to a rules file it just helped write. Push back on anything that doesn't match your sense of the work.

Each round the agent turns the work into sharper rules and drops what the work disproved: do the work → capture → reflect → sharpen. Repeat on every rules file.

Get a cold read

Then, use a cold critic. Ask the agent to open a second, independent reader with only the site as context.

Prompt (Cowork)

Launch a fresh subagent to give an unbiased read on `module-1/site.html`. The agent should read it cold, with no memory of building it.

Have the agent answer:
1. Quote the one line that feels most uniquely this person (not the best line, the most UNIQUELY them).
2. Quote the most generic line that could be copy-pasted from anyone's site.

Where the critic sees generic, your context is thin: add one sharp detail, then regenerate the site. Where its "uniquely you" pick matches your own read, you're on solid ground. Your read outweighs the agent's.

Key Concepts

  • Context is the brush: what you give the agent shapes the output.
  • Output got specific because the context did.
  • Guardrails are context you can reuse.
  • Your domain expertise is the test.

Bring to Module 2

Bring a live challenge. Do the linked Module 2 prework first.

Pre-reads before Module 2

Lecture

Before the Memory

What you do:

Bring one live challenge, check what the agent can read about it, use a plan-first control, and leave yourself a three-line readiness note.

Module 2 works on real history: meetings, notes, decisions, half-written documents.

Bring one live challenge

Module 2 builds a memory: a folder of notes and source material the agent reads before answering. Bring a real challenge: a decision you're making, a bet you're placing, or work whose direction is still unclear.

Pick one open enough to need thought, narrow enough for 5-8 topic pages.

If stuck, scan your next two weeks of calendar; the biggest unresolved item is usually your challenge.

Check what the agent can read

Module 2 works best when the agent can read a source connected to your challenge. If your work lives in a wiki or document system, check that the agent can reach it. Your own files work too.

Connectors link the agent to places where your work lives: Confluence, SharePoint, OneDrive, Google Drive, or whatever you use. Look for them in your runtime's connector settings.

Without a connector, the memory can start from files and pasted excerpts in your training directory.

Put a plan before action

Module 2 has the agent create and update multiple files. Ask it for a plan first, then approve or revise it. Runtimes offer this as a mode or via the prompt.

Use it when the next step may write several files or edit anything you care about. Skip it for quick one-turn work.

Pick one:

  • Ask the agent which planning control your runtime offers, then try it on a harmless file change.
  • Watch Matt Pocock's video about planning before execution.

Start the Module 2 handoff

Create prework/module-2-start.md in your training directory. Add:

  • the live challenge you are bringing;
  • the first source the agent can read about it, or your fallback;
  • the planning control you will use before the agent writes files.

Module 2 builds ./challenge.md from these lines. If a line is blank, name a fallback; do not fill it with a plausible answer.

Read the memory frame

Read Karpathy's LLM Wiki gist for the mental model: a useful system is a living pile of text the agent can read, maintain, and improve. Your memory starts as plain text, which the agent reads and rewrites easily.

Bring to Module 2: prework/module-2-start.md.

Save the prework, end this session, then start Module 2 fresh at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Next

Your rules file already carries what you learned into the next session. Module 2 grows that into a memory for one real challenge.

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Building Agent Systems

Big Idea

A system remembers, grows, and compounds around the one thing you need to make progress on. Chat can't.

Prework

Module 2 prework. (1) Bring a live challenge. (2) Optional: connect your work wiki or document store. (3) Plan-mode primer.Plan-first primer. (4) Karpathy's LLM Wiki post. (5) Optional: Lindenberg memory-architecture piece.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Create agent memory
  • Create an agent
  • Schedule an agent
  • Review an agent's plan

Start here

Start a fresh session or task at ~/Documents/agents-101/. Module 1's scrollback stays behind.

Your memory/, sources/ and agents/ folders are empty from prework. Module 1's files stay out of this build. You develop your working rules in the Debrief. The existing root file only loads course navigation.

What's the difference between asking an agent a question and having an agent keep a knowledge base that every later agent reads?

Name the challenge you're carrying

What challenge are you carrying that isn't solved yet? Not a task. You'll build a memory around it.

If everything you've read and drafted on that challenge moved into a memory an agent could read and sharpen, what changes at work?

Connectors let the agent combine clues that live apart, like a wiki page and an email thread.

Lecture

Demo: 1st scheduled agent

One scheduled agent reads work context, follows one hard guardrail, and writes an output you can inspect. The context might be a calendar, a short note, or a file in the training folder.

The guardrail: propose or draft only, do not send, edit, book, or change anything. The schedule makes the agent run again without a fresh prompt and write the next result in the same place.

Exercise

Exercise: Name your next big challenge

Time: 15 minutes.

Session (new, "Module 2 - Building agent systems")

What you do:

Pin one real problem before building. The memory you build is a folder of notes and sources the agent reads before answering.

Pick your next big challenge.

An initiative you own and work on in these weeks, one that produces work (memo, plan, decision, brief, campaign, rollout).

Good: The Q2 pricing redesign: usage-based vs. seats, pilot cohort, sales briefing.

Not a fit: last year's re-org, becoming a better leader, understanding AI.

Write the brief.

The agent interviews you with three questions, one at a time, and writes ./challenge.md.

Prompt (Cowork)

I'm in a training where I'll build a working memory around one live challenge I'm wrestling with. Help me pin the challenge down. Ask me these in turn:

1. In one sentence, what's the initiative? A real, midsized-to-large piece of work you're carrying over the next few weeks — scope, stakes, still open.
2. What have you already tried, read, or decided? What's ruled out, what's still open?
3. Where are you currently stuck on this — what's the specific part you can't seem to get past, or the question you keep asking yourself and not landing?

When I've answered all three, write a one-paragraph brief to ./challenge.md. Show it to me before saving.

Exercise

Exercise: Build your challenge memory

Time: 47 minutes.

What you do:

Build a memory around your next big challenge at work, pinned in ./challenge.md: the board paper due in three weeks, the re-org you're shaping. Keep it narrow enough that 5–8 topic pages cover it.

The empty sources/, memory/, and agents/ folders are in place from prework. Keep the same session running.

Phase 1: Curate, ingest, build

20 min

Three beats: the agent helps you curate a plan, pulls in (or points at) the content for sources/, then builds memory/ from what's on disk.

Always comply with your company's AI policy. Its rules on what can go through an LLM hold here. If in doubt, check before uploading.

Ease yourself in. Bring only what you'd share with a smart assistant without a second thought. If a thread, deck or doc feels sensitive, skip it.

Approve the plan before the files change

Several phases re-read sources/ or memory/ and rewrite multiple files. Ask for a plan first.

If the agent starts reading before showing the plan, stop it, steer narrower, say "continue". For something simple, cap it: "10 sources max".

Curate the source plan

Beat 1. Curate. The agent surveys what's available and asks about your world.

Prompt (Cowork)

I'm building a knowledge memory for one specific challenge I'm working on. Do this in three beats:

1. Check what connectors are enabled right now. Name the ones you can reach (wiki, docs, storage, chat, email) and the ones that would be useful but aren't connected.

2. Then ask me where my work material actually lives. Don't assume Confluence or OneDrive — ask what's in my world: my team's wiki (whatever the tool), my shared drives and docs, email threads, chat channels, personal notes, favourite practitioner blogs. Get specific: tool names, the 2–3 most relevant spaces/folders, the people I've been exchanging on this challenge.
   Ask one question at a time. Wait for my answer before asking the next. Do not show me the question list.

3. Then propose a curation plan covering three kinds of material: (a) internal knowledge — which searches in which tools, (b) recent work — which threads, folders, decks, (c) outside-in — 2–3 working practitioners or specific articles worth reading (not vendor blogs).

Two rules for the plan. First: only recommend sources I would feel comfortable sharing with an LLM today. If something is likely to be sensitive — board material, personal emails, customer data, HR records — flag it as "skip for now, revisit after Module 4" rather than putting it in the plan. Second: curate only the paths and spaces I actually name. If you spot nearby material I didn't name — a sibling folder, other files in the same drive — list what you see and ask before including any of it. Never pull it in on your own. I'll push back where the plan is off.

If something is likely to be sensitive — board material, personal emails, customer data, HR records — flag it as "skip for now, revisit after Module 4" rather than putting it in the plan. Second: curate only the paths and spaces I actually name. If you spot nearby material I didn't name — a sibling folder, other files in the same drive — list what you see and ask before including any of it. Never pull it in on your own. I'll push back where the plan is off.

Push back, sharpen, add what's missing.

Ingest the sources

Beat 2. Ingest. The agent pulls in the content for sources/.

What the agent reads. The CLI agent reads any path you name; use absolute paths outside the training folder.The desktop agent reads files you attach; attach outside sources before sending.The agent reads your selected working folders; add a folder or attach a file for one message.

Prompt (Cowork)

For every source in the curation plan we just agreed, create one file in sources/. Use the best method per source:

- Publicly fetchable URL (practitioner blog, public article)? Fetch the page, save the text as sources/<slug>.md with a header naming URL + title + why-it's-relevant.
- Reachable via a connector you have (wiki, docs, drive)? Pull the content through and save the same way.
- Local file on my laptop at a path I named? Save sources/<slug>.md as a reference — absolute path + title + why-it's-relevant, no copied content. You'll read the actual file directly when Beat 3 needs it.
- Behind a connector you can't reach, or in a tool you don't have? Save sources/<slug>.md as a reference too — URL or path + title + why-it's-relevant + "NOT REACHABLE — share with me when you want this included." Don't ask me to paste anything; if I want it included, I'll share the file.

Create files only for the sources in the plan we agreed. If you come across other material while you work — files I didn't name, a folder you weren't pointed at — don't add it; note what you saw and I'll decide whether it belongs.

When done, tell me the three lists: (1) fetched and saved as content, (2) linked by local path, (3) not reachable — waiting for me to attach. I'll attach whatever I want to include before we build the memory.

Build the memory under a plan

Beat 3. Build memory. Ask the agent to write a plan first and wait for your approval before it touches files.

Prompt (Cowork)

Read every real-content file in sources/. For each major topic you find, create a markdown file in memory/ with a clear title, 3–5 key claims, and an "open questions" section for things the sources disagree on or leave unclear. Then write memory/index.md that links to every topic page with a one-line description.

Rules — non-negotiable:

1. Sources first, always. Every memory page derives from real content — either a sources/ file with content inline, or a sources/ reference file that links to a local path (read the linked file directly when you need it). Skip sources/ files marked "NOT REACHABLE" and any empty placeholder files. If no real content is reachable yet, stop and tell me before writing anything in memory/.

2. Every claim ends with a citation in the form `[sources/<filename>]` pointing to the file it came from. One claim, one source file, on the same line. If a claim has no source, don't write it — put the gap in "open questions" instead. I'll spot-check citations against the files.

3. Distinctive, not descriptive. Extract what's specific to my situation — my company, my sources, my challenge. If a claim could appear in a competitor's memory on the same kind of problem, it's too generic; rewrite or cut.

Review the plan, then have the memory audit itself

Read the plan. If two topics should merge or something is missing, give one sentence of feedback and ask for a revised plan. Otherwise approve.

Then ask the agent to audit itself:

If on re-reading all three are specific, say why, and name the sentence most at risk of slipping generic. List the generic ones in memory/soft-pages.md.

Phase 2: Your first custom agent

10 min

A custom agent is a markdown file of instructions: its purpose and rules.

Prompt (Cowork)

Help me create my first custom agent as a markdown file in agents/. Ask me these one at a time. Wait for my answer before asking the next. Do not show me the question list.

1. What recurring job should this agent do for my challenge? One sentence — e.g., "draft a next-step memo for my CEO," "surface three risks for next week's stakeholder meeting," "synthesize three talking points on progress so far."
2. What rules matter? Starter rules: cite the memory file for every claim, never invent, ask when a source is thin, keep my voice. Change at least one so it's actually mine. Include any hard lines — things the agent must not do even if asked.

Pick a filename from the job. Show me the file before saving.

Phase 3: Compound

7 min

A good knowledge base sharpens: pages get tighter as new sources arrive, not longer.

Pick one source that fills a gap (an article, a skipped doc, a local file). Paste its link or path after the New source: line.

Prompt (Cowork)

Take the source below and integrate it into the memory. Steps:

1. Read the source. Integrate its claims into existing pages (sharpen, don't append). Drop any claim the source contradicts. For new topics, add pages in the existing shape. Update memory/index.md.
2. Rewrite tops in place. Replace old framing; don't preserve it above a new section.

When you're done, tell me three pages that got sharper (not longer) and one claim that got dropped or replaced.

Phase 5: Close, put it to work

6 min

Ask your memory the hardest open question on your challenge, not "summarize the sources." For example: "What's the strongest argument for option A over option B?" "Where does our current plan break if the market shifts?"

Ask it twice, once to a helper agent in an empty folder, the way a chat answers, and once through the agent you built in Phase 2; both answers go side by side into module-2/close.md.

Prompt (Cowork)

Answer my question below twice and save both answers in module-2/close.md, under the headings Bare and System.

1. Bare: dispatch a helper agent in an empty scratch folder with only the question. No memory, no rules, no files.
2. System: run the question through the agent I built in Phase 2, using my memory and its rules, citing the memory file each claim came from. Mark any line that used the source I added in Phase 3.

End close.md with one line: what the System answer has that the Bare one could not. Then add the gap the System answer still left to the open questions of the memory page it belongs to.

Take stock of the system you built

What happened:

A memory is files you keep, not a thread you close.

The point:

A system is persistence (files it reads again) plus automation (it runs). Together they compound: each cycle starts from what the last one left.

This was Recipe 2: sources, memory, rules file. For your next challenge, the Cookbook for Agent System Design holds the same moves.

Lecture

Compounding

The thing a chat can't do is Phase 3: new sources made the existing topic pages sharper instead of longer. The second batch made the first batch better. That is compounding.

A few problems, or a capability?

We started building an agent factory. Three people went off and deployed agents, fast. I asked what capabilities they were building. They said: we have a few problems to solve.

Solve a problem and close it, and problem four costs what problem one did. Keep what each one taught in files the next run reads, and problem four starts ahead. That is the difference between a chat and a system.

Stop chatting. Build a system.

I keep repeating this. In a chat you handhold the agent, take a few actions, and at the end nothing is saved. Your performance is about the next hundred sessions, not this one.

Two words, held together

A system is two things stacked:

  • Persistence. Files on disk the agent reads again, not a thread that resets.
  • Automation. The instructions sit in a file the agent reads at session start.

A saved document with no agent is just a document. An agent with no files is a chat. Together, the system keeps getting better the more you feed it.

Why the sharpening happens

The agent read the existing topic pages first, as context, then the new sources, then integrated. Old and new claims met, and the ones that couldn't survive got cut. Context shapes output, at system scale.

It gets better by being edited

Keep the rules small and boring. Apply them consistently across thousands of small updates, and let the compounding do the work.

A folder of text, and that is the point

The memory is a folder of markdown files. No database, special tool or paid tier is needed.

The agent in agents/ is also markdown: instructions a session reads when you point it there. Any agent runtime can read it.

Language models are strongest at reading and writing text. Stored as text, knowledge is read by reading and updated by writing.

Three layers, one folder

Three layers, separate on purpose. Raw sources: the untouched originals you dropped in. Memory: topic pages the agent maintains and sharpens. Rules file: the instructions the agent reads so every update follows the same pattern.

Sharpen the memory, never the sources, or you lose the evidence.

What this unlocks

The agent's answers cite your files and carry a voice that isn't a generic industry take. Generic AI becomes your AI when you build the memory it reads.

Could a competitor claim this?

If a competitor could claim a page, the memory is growing but not compounding. Spot what's still generic and sharpen it.

It can only use what someone wrote down

The agent works only from what is in its context: the session and the files it reads. Most of what you know about your company sits in heads and corridors, and nobody has written it down.

Every round moves one more piece of that knowledge out of your head and into files the agent reads next session.

Debrief

Five minutes. A retro, and your own working rules for this directory. The agent writes the rules every agent here reads: what worked, what rubbed, what got repeated.

Prompt (Cowork)

Review this session and write the first version of CLAUDE.md at the training-directory root. The evidence: ./challenge.md, every file in sources/ (scan titles + first lines), every file in memory/, and our conversation.

The rules file governs how agents behave in this directory from now on — how memory gets compiled, how sources are treated, what claims require citations, what counts as "specific to my challenge" vs. generic. Don't invent — extract. Every rule you write should be traceable to a specific moment in the session where the rule either helped or would have helped.

Structure however makes sense for how we actually worked today — section headers, short paragraphs, bullets where a list is clearest. No retro-notes framing; write the rules as if they'd always been the rules. Cover at minimum: the memory (when and how pages get written, what grounds them), the sources (what they are, whether they're editable), the agents (how they relate to the memory), and whatever else earned its place.

When you're done, tell me in 3–5 lines: the rules you wrote, which session moments grounded each one, and what you chose NOT to include and why. Be specific on the omissions: name at least one session moment where you considered a rule and skipped it, and the reason. I shouldn't have to open the file to know what's in it.

Push back on the summary

Push back on anything in the agent's summary that doesn't match your sense of the work. "Keep the draft I accepted as an example, beside the fixes." "You missed the bit where we had to regenerate three times because of X."

What the agent leaves out is often the signal. A summary that names three rules and skips the messy fourth, where you re-prompted twice, is the tell.

Fix the output, then fix the rule

Your agent is "right" when it works. A miss that comes back on a rerun is context the agent still lacks: sharpen the memory, tighten a rule, rewrite the prompt. You spot the next mistakes by running the system and watching where it bends.

Watching where it bends is continuous improvement, done by hand.

The model will change under this

The model will change. Your memory will not.

Your folder holds your challenge, your sources and your rules. A better model reads your folder better.

Key Concepts

  • A system compounds around your challenge: each new source sharpens what is already there. A chat starts from zero.
  • Persistence plus automation: a system.
  • Three layers in plain text: untouched raw sources, a memory the agent sharpens, a rules file.

Bring to Module 3

A daily agent, scheduled, with a week of observation behind it. It reads your challenge memory. In Module 3, several agents work on that same memory.

Exercise

Exercise: Your first scheduled agent

Time: 35 minutes to set up. One glance a day for a week.

What you do:

Put a scheduled agent in front of your memory. Each morning it reads the memory and tells you something useful.

Pick one of three jobs:

  • Morning plan: reads memory and calendar, writes a 5-line plan naming which meetings move the challenge and which are noise
  • Daily risk scan: reads memory, flags the assumption most likely wrong or the question open longest
  • Next move: reads memory, drafts one action: a message, a question, or a small decision for today

Pick the one you would read tomorrow morning.

Phase 1: Connect any data the job needs

8 min

For the morning-plan job, enable Google Calendar or Microsoft Outlook Calendar in your agent runtime's connector settings and sign in with your work account. Without a connector, use a calendar screenshot or exported agenda. The other two jobs need no connector.

Phase 2: Capture the look

7 min

Give your daily output the look of your company's website, or any site you like: colours, typography, headers, voice. The agent extracts the pattern into a plain-language style file on disk and reuses it by name, like the memory.

Prompt (Cowork)

Look at my company's website. I'll give you a URL or paste a key page when you ask. Extract the visual pattern — primary and accent colours (with hex codes), font families, header shape, spacing, overall tone of voice. Write it to ./style.md at the training-directory root, in plain language (not a CSS file). Short and practical: a designer reading ./style.md should be able to produce something that looks like our site without visiting it.

Then append one line to my root CLAUDE.md under a new "Styling" heading: "When producing HTML output, follow style.md."

Show me both files before saving.

Phase 4: Schedule it

6 min

Open the Schedule sidebar in the desktop app and click New task → New local task:

  • Name: Morning memory
  • Frequency: Daily at 7:00 AM, or the time you want it to fire
  • Prompt: the scheduling prompt below. It writes the daily output to latest.html.

Prompt (Agent workspace)

Read module-2/morning-agent/morning.md and run the job. Read the current state of memory/ as context. Follow the rules in that file and in the root CLAUDE.md. Write the output to module-2/morning-agent/latest.html.

Save, then click Run now once. Double-click module-2/morning-agent/latest.html to open it in your browser. To fix anything, edit module-2/morning-agent/morning.md or ./style.md. The scheduling prompt names both files, so tomorrow's run picks up the change.

Phase 5: Let it run for a week

4 min

For the first three days, don't retune. Open module-2/morning-agent/latest.html each morning and watch for:

  • Useful days: what made them work?
  • Comical or wrong days: what was missing from the memory?
  • Claims you, the domain expert, know are off: your next memory edits.
  • Styling drift from your company site: sharpen ./style.md.
  • Who else would read this output, and what would make them open it?

Turn the memory into a running loop

What happened:

Each morning's output shows what is sharp and what is soft in your memory.

The point:

A memory an agent reads on a schedule, producing output you respond to, is the start of a loop. Every HTML agent you build looks native to your organisation, because the root instructions file points each agent to ./style.md.

Exercise

Exercise: Prework before Module 3

Time: 40 minutes total. 25 reading, 5 noting takeaways, 10 on the helper-agent primer.

What you do:

Two reads. Both prime moves the Module 3 exercise leans on. Neither asks you to build anything.

Reading 1. Five practitioners, automating their work.

See what a single agent already does for working practitioners who've folded coding agents into daily research, writing, and shipping.

Pick three. Read one piece each.

  1. Simon Willison. Browse his current coding-agent field notes. Pick one worked example where he shows the prompt, artifact, test, or correction rather than only announcing a feature.
  2. Edward Harker. Read his coding-agent operating notes (16 May 2026). Look for the operating routine around the agent, not a magic prompt.
  3. Armin Ronacher. Read The Coming Loop (23 June 2026). Notice what changes when the human designs the loop and its feedback instead of driving every step.
  4. Thariq Shihipar. Read The unreasonable effectiveness of HTML (20 May 2026). Track why changing the review artifact changes how closely the human stays in the work.
  5. Daniel Bilsborough. Read The Practitioner's Guide to Coding Agents (updated 6 August 2026). Look for the plain-text memory and the boundary where consequential work still needs a person.

For each pick, note in plain language: what is this person automating that they used to do by hand, and what's the move that made it work? Three bullets, one per practitioner. Keep the note somewhere you'll see on training day.

The aim is to calibrate how much one agent can already do, so you know what coordinating three more buys you.

Reading 2. Helper agents, in plain language.

Module 3 Phase 2 spawns three helper agents in one session or task.

What it is. A helper agent is one the lead agent dispatches to do one focused job. It gets:

  • its own instructions (what it's for, what rules it follows);
  • its own context window (a clean slate, so its work doesn't clutter yours);
  • access to the same filesystem (it reads and writes in your working directory, same as the lead session or task).

When the job is done, the helper returns a single result to the lead agent and disappears. Several can run in parallel.

How to launch one. Ask the lead agent in plain language: "Launch a helper agent to review the three retrieval files and write its take to module-3/stances/planner.md." For several at once: "Launch these three helper agents in parallel," and list them. The lead agent waits for all three to return, then continues.

What you'll see. Your runtime shows a running task or agent entry with a short description for each helper. In Phase 2, each helper writes a stance file to module-3/stances/ as it completes.

What you don't need. No agent definition file and no special command. Plain-language prompting is enough for Phase 2.

For the full reference, open the Claude Code helper-agent documentationopen the Codex helper-agent documentationopen the GitHub Copilot subagent documentationopen the in-app help and search for agents. You're after the shape: helper with instructions, own context, returns a result. You summon it by asking.

What to bring to Module 3: the three one-line practitioner takeaways.

Save the run, then end this session.

Next

Before the next module, have the agent build a few more agents you need. Pick by pain: a task you keep doing manually. Meeting prep and calendar triage are fine starters. Keep the first version proposal-only: the agent drafts, ranks, or prepares; you decide what leaves the system.

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Multi-Agent Systems

Big Idea

Several agents can work on one problem together. Split the work, run the agents in parallel, and let them hand off through shared files. Three agents search, three more decide. Handoffs are where work gets lost, so check them.

Prework

Schedule your personal agent to read your challenge memory for a week. What is an Agent covers tools, memory and context. Helper agents primer before Module 3.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Orchestrate multiple agents
  • Split work across agents
  • Debug agent handoffs

Start here

Start a fresh session or task at ~/Documents/agents-101/. Save outputs under module-3/.

Three agents search Confluence, OneDrive and practitioner articles, and three more decide what it means.

Lecture

Demo: Agent that takes action

The scheduled agent runs with one new permission: post one message to a demo Slack channel.

The message holds no customer data, private names, commitments or decisions. The agent writes the message first and sends only after approval. If the channel is missing or the message needs judgment, the agent stops.

Writing a file changes your folder. Slack changes another system.

Exercise: Name your crux

Session (new, "Module 3 - Multi-agent systems")

What you do:

Ask the agent to read Module 2's memory/ and name the crux, Richard Rumelt's term for the one thing that, if solved, releases pressure on everything else. Push back when the first answer restates the problem.

Prompt (Cowork)

Look at my challenge memory. Find the load-bearing obstacle: the one thing that, if solved, unlocks the others. Richard Rumelt calls this the "crux."

Rules:
- Not a problem restatement. "We need to build credibility" is a goal, not a crux. "Prospects won't meet us until someone they trust vouches" IS a crux: it names the mechanism that blocks everything else.
- Not a category. "Positioning is unclear" is a category. "Buyers can't tell in 30 seconds whether we sell training or consulting" is specific enough to act on.
- Test it: if this obstacle moved, would at least three other stuck things release? If not, keep looking. It isn't the crux.

Exercise

Exercise: Three retrievers, one curator

Time: ~28 minutes.

Three retrievers fetch raw material on your challenge into sources/; a fourth session curates it into memory/. All read ./crux.md. Each session has its own context and connectors. Skip any retriever you can't run today.

Keep your crux session as Session 4 (synthesizer). Open three more: 1 wiki, 2 docs, 3 internet.

In Cowork, keep your crux task as Task 4 and start three more: 1 wiki, 2 docs, 3 internet.

Paste each retriever prompt and confirm its short list. If an agent starts reading the world, stop it, steer narrower, then say "continue".

Session 1, wiki: sources/wiki-retrieval.md.

Prompt (Cowork)

You are the wiki retriever for my challenge. Your job: find every piece of internal wiki material that matters to ./crux.md (the crux you named in the opening, plus the ## Question section). Read the question first.

Then:
1. Propose 6–8 search terms for my team's wiki. Confluence, Notion, SharePoint wiki, Guru, whichever I use. Ask me to confirm or sharpen them before running anything, and ask which wiki to target if it's ambiguous.
2. Run the searches through my wiki connector. Open the pages. Read them properly.
3. Append each finding to sources/wiki-retrieval.md as soon as you have it, one paragraph per finding, naming the page/space and one line on why this matters for the question. Never overwrite earlier findings. Keep only what speaks to the question; don't summarise the wiki.
4. End the file with a "Conflicts and gaps" section: where internal pages disagree, where the wiki is thin, what's conspicuously missing.

Write each finding as soon as you have it; don't batch until the end. The synthesizer in another session reads `sources/` continuously — streaming writes keep it busy.

No need to update `memory/` — another session is handling curation. Just write to `sources/`.

Sources first. Every finding cites the specific page title and URL you actually opened. If you can't find a source for a claim, write "[NOT FOUND]", do not fill from prior knowledge. If a search returns nothing, say so; don't invent page titles.

Session 4, synthesizer: memory/.

Prompt (Cowork)

No plan or preamble — enter the loop now.

You are the synthesizer for my challenge. Three retrievers are running concurrently in Sessions 1, 2, and 3 — they'll write findings to sources/wiki-retrieval.md, sources/docs-retrieval.md, and sources/internet-retrieval.md as they finish. Your job is curation: integrate those findings into my memory/ topic pages, scoped to ./crux.md (the crux you named in the opening, plus the ## Question section).

Memory is curated, not a raw dump. Existing topic pages cover the challenge — extend them where the new sources sharpen what's already there; create a new topic page where the retrievals reveal a topic memory was missing. Cite sources by filename + paragraph.

The loop:
1. Wait for any new content in sources/. When a file appears (or grows), read it.
2. Diff against existing memory/ pages. Extend in place if the topic exists; create a new page if it doesn't. Don't ask permission for either path.
3. Make the update. Cite the source file by name. Integrate, don't append. Keep claims tight.
4. Repeat until all three retrievals are integrated.

When all three retrievals are in: write a one-paragraph note at memory/_synthesis-m3.md. List each memory file you actually changed by name and the exact filenames git diff would show; if fewer changed than the retrieval count, say so explicitly. Name where retrievals contradicted what was already in memory by quoting the conflicting claims verbatim from each source. That contradiction line is load-bearing — flag it, don't smooth it.

Don't fabricate. Every memory update cites a source-file finding. If a retrieval is empty or thin, say so in your synthesis note rather than papering over the gap.

2. Diff against existing memory/ pages. Extend in place if the topic exists; create a new page if it doesn't. Don't ask permission for either path.
3. Make the update. Cite the source file by name. Integrate, don't append. Keep claims tight.
4. Repeat until all three retrievals are integrated.

When all three retrievals are in: write a one-paragraph note at memory/_synthesis-m3.md. List each memory file you actually changed by name and the exact filenames git diff would show; if fewer changed than the retrieval count, say so explicitly. Name where retrievals contradicted what was already in memory by quoting the conflicting claims verbatim from each source. That contradiction line is load-bearing — flag it, don't smooth it.

Don't fabricate. Every memory update cites a source-file finding. If a retrieval is empty or thin, say so in your synthesis note rather than papering over the gap.

Exercise

Exercise: Three minds, one synthesis

Time: ~22 minutes.

What you do: Spawn three helpers with different stances on your curated memory.

Stay in the session that wrote ./crux.md, close the retriever sessions, and wait for memory/_synthesis-m3.md. If a helper reads too widely, stop it, steer narrower, then say "continue".

Ask the agent to spawn three helpers with different stances, then apply Rumelt's kernel to synthesize their notes into ./crux.md.

Prompt (Claude Code Desktop)

Start dispatching immediately. No plan or preamble.

Spawn three subagents in parallel, each with a different stance. Each reads my curated memory/ (the layer the previous exercise integrated the retrievals into) and writes a short note (under 200 words) to module-3/stances/.

Subagent 1: Backward-from-end planner. Imagine the outcome we want in 12 months. Work backwards. What must be true by month 9, month 6, month 3, next week? What's the first move on Monday?

Subagent 2: Assumption experimenter. Roger Martin's test: for the most attractive option, what would have to be true for it to work? List the load-bearing assumptions. For each, name the cheapest test that could kill it within a week.

Subagent 3: Counterintuitive reframer. What's the obvious answer here? Now, what's the reframe? Question the framing of the question itself. Steal an analogy from an unrelated field. Which bias is operating, and what happens if we invert it? (Be sharp, not glib.)

When the three return, show me the stances side by side, unsummarised, so I read them as three voices. Tell me where memory had conflicts or gaps that weakened any stance.

Then synthesize. Apply Rumelt's strategy kernel — diagnosis (what's really going on, in plain language), guiding policy (one coherent approach that addresses the diagnosis), coherent actions (3–5 concrete moves that follow). Append only a new `## Answer` section to ./crux.md with the three legs; do not modify existing sections. Name where the three stances disagreed and which one you sided with and why; don't smooth the disagreement. Show me before saving.

Lecture

Lecture: How agents work together

Six agents worked on one question in this module. Three searched, three decided. None of them talked to each other. They handed off through shared files.

Agents hand off through shared files

Each agent writes what it found to a file. The next agent reads the file, not the other agent's mind: sources/ held the search, module-3/stances/ held the three takes, crux.md holds the answer.

A file can be read later: by you, by another agent, by next week's run. A conversation between agents cannot.

Split the work, run it in parallel

Split the problem where its parts differ: a different source, a different dialect, a different stance. Give each part its own agent. Bring the parts back to one place that decides.

Three agents searched in parallel. Three argued from different seats. One session applied the kernel and committed.

Two ways to run a team

Separate sessions. Each agent keeps its own context, tools and clock. You see each one work and can step into one without confusing the others.

Helper agents in one session. Quick parallel thinking with a bounded return. The main session starts each helper, gives it one job, and discards it when its file comes back.

A framework makes it pick

Without a framework, the synthesizer summarises three views, evenly weighted.

Hand the synthesizer the strategy kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions). The synthesizer then commits to one diagnosis and drops what does not serve it.

Handoffs are where work gets lost

Every split creates a handoff, and handoffs are where work goes wrong. A retriever finds two numbers and the curator keeps one. A source's internal shorthand is rewritten in public tone and loses its meaning.

Open the files where one agent handed to the next. An error made there stacks through the steps after it.

Split for a reason

Not every job needs a team. Could one prompt produce the same quality? Then write that one prompt.

Split where the parts cannot be one agent: different access, a different dialect, a different stance. One agent per recurring workflow; a team only where the workflow divides.

Lecture

Debugging Stuck Agents

Agents get stuck: wrong source, three views averaged into mush, the wrong file written, confident right before a failed handoff.

Diagnose before repair

Prompt your stuck system to diagnose whether the bug lives in the sources, the processing, or the boundary between agents.

Prompt (Cowork)

Find the root cause of this bug.

Read the relevant files and the recent session context. Tell me whether the failure is mainly:
1. a source problem: missing, stale, contradictory, or unread evidence
2. a processing problem: wrong prompt, wrong role, bad handoff, vague output shape, or synthesis that averaged away disagreement
3. a boundary problem: the agent tried to use data, tools, or authority it should not have had

Do not fix anything yet. Show me the failure chain in 5 bullets: what happened, where it started, where it became visible, what file or prompt caused it, and the smallest fix that would prevent the next run.

Make your own variant.

Sources, processing, boundary

  1. Sources: add the missing file, remove the stale one, split contradictory material so the agent sees the conflict.

  2. Processing: rewrite the prompt, role, handoff, or output format. Split an agent doing two jobs.

  3. Boundary: narrow the agent's job, remove the tool, add a human gate, move the risky step from "do" to "propose."

  4. Shrink the rerun: rerun only the smallest step that should now differ.

  5. Have the agent write the lesson: a rule for the root instructions file on what to read first, what not to smooth over, which output format to produce, and when to stop and ask.

Debrief

Five minutes. The agent reviews the four prompts, the retrieval files, the synthesizer's briefing and the conversation, then rewrites the root instructions file in place and reports what changed. Push back on anything off.

Prompt (Cowork)

Start by reading the files. No plan or preamble.

Review this session and update the rules. Read CLAUDE.md at the root, then scan what we just produced: agents/, sources/, module-3/. Audit harshly. Diplomatic summaries are a failing grade here. Look back over the session: where did agents step on each other, where did context get dropped at a handoff, where did one retriever's dialect leak into the synthesizer, where did the three stances collapse into a single voice, where did one agent need to be two (or two to be one)?

Then rewrite CLAUDE.md. Integrate, don't append. Sharpen the rules that govern division of work and handoff shape: what each agent is for, what it writes to, what it does NOT do. Add what's missing, remove what turned out wrong. Don't add a "retro notes" section; rewrite the file as the better version.

When you're done, tell me in 3-5 lines: what you added, what you sharpened, what you removed, and why. Name at least TWO handoff seams where the rules wobbled, with specific evidence: name the file, the pass, and what was lost. Name one thing you would have missed without the "audit harshly" instruction. A seam without evidence doesn't count.

Then rewrite CLAUDE.md. Integrate, don't append. Sharpen the rules that govern division of work and handoff shape: what each agent is for, what it writes to, what it does NOT do. Add what's missing, remove what turned out wrong. Don't add a "retro notes" section; rewrite the file as the better version.

When you're done, tell me in 3-5 lines: what you added, what you sharpened, what you removed, and why. Name at least TWO handoff seams where the rules wobbled, with specific evidence: name the file, the pass, and what was lost. Name one thing you would have missed without the "audit harshly" instruction. A seam without evidence doesn't count.

Key Concepts

  • Agents work together through shared files: what one writes is the next one's context.
  • Split where the parts differ, run them in parallel, bring them back to one place that decides.
  • Sessions on shared files, or helpers the main session starts and discards.
  • Handoffs are where work gets lost: open the files where one agent handed to the next.

Pre-reads before Module 4

Agent Trigger List, After Module 3 and the multi-agent sections of What is an Agent.

Lecture

Reading: Before Module 4

Reading 1. Personal skills. A skill is a SKILL.md plus supporting files (policy text, templates). The SKILL.md says what the skill is for, when to use it, and how. The agent loads it when a task matches. In Module 4 you run your policy files raw, package the check with a policy lens and an agent-risk lens, then run it on your Module 2-3 system.

Reading 2. Agent risk sits on top of normal security. Network controls, access rights and audit logs still apply. Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound. Also watch secrets in context, tool confusion and skill supply-chain.

Before Module 4: jot three to five lines on what matters about the data you work with, e.g. "Sales never lets unredacted CRM exports leave the building."

After the optional check and pre-reads, end this session. Module 4 starts fresh at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Bring to Module 4: what's the worst thing it could do with that access?

An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.

Next

Until Module 4, keep working on your real problem: add an agent for a critical dependency, or a plan visualisation.

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Security

Big Idea

You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output. Run a check; don't wait for certainty.

Prework

Read the Agent Trigger List, After Module 3, the multi-agent sections of What is an Agent, and Before Module 4.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Audit an agent for security
  • Write a skill
  • Mitigate agent risk

Start here

Start a fresh session or task at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

The agent reads the Module 3 system, the root instructions file, and the policy files under module-4/policies/. Reports go to outputs/.

Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.

How its text becomes an action.

Prompt (Cowork)

You write text. How does that text become actions in other systems?

You write text. How does that text become actions in other systems?

Read the answers as mechanism. Each tool has a name, a description and an input format. The context makes one description look relevant, and the model writes a structured request. The harness turns that text into an action, and the tool does the work.

A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action. If the tool description is vague, the context misleading or the request aimed at the wrong system, the action inherits the problem.

Exercise

Exercise: Run and package a security skill

Time: 40 minutes. Phase 1 ~10, Phase 2 ~8, Phase 3 ~22.

Session (new, "Module 4 - Security skill")

Start a new agent session at your training-directory root.Start a new Cowork task with your training-directory root as the working folder.

Name it m4-security-skill if your runtime supports session names.

What you do: Run the policy files raw against your system from modules 2-3, then package the useful move into one skill with two lenses. Stop when the skill exists.

A skill packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent loads when the work matches. You run it again instead of re-prompting from memory.

Phase 3: Author both lenses

22 min

The skill is a SKILL.md plus any reference files, with two lenses: company policy, and agent risk (what the agent can reach, what it might leak, what a misleading prompt or source might make it do).

Ask the agent to author both lenses and name the risk patterns the agent-security lens covers. Expect many questions over several rounds.

Prompt (Cowork)

Author the reusable security check now. Two lenses.

Build one reusable skill source under module-4/skills/agent-audit/. The main file is SKILL.md. It contains both lenses: POLICY and AGENT-SECURITY. Add supporting reference files only where useful.



Lens 1 - POLICY. Rules drawn from everything in module-4/policies/ plus the lines I just typed. For each rule, the lens produces one row in a report: rule name, one-line description, verdict (compliant / violating / "I can't tell"), one line of evidence from the target system. The verdict column stays plain - "I can't tell" is a real answer.

Lens 2 - AGENT-SECURITY. Check what the agent can reach, what sensitive material might stay in its context, and what could go wrong because ordinary text can act like an instruction. The lens MUST cover these named risk patterns by name:

- prompt injection (direct - hostile input in a user prompt; indirect - hostile content in a retrieved source the agent reads)
- secrets in context and scrollback (API keys, customer data, partner-NDA material persisting in the transcript or the agent's working memory)
- tool confusion (agent invokes the wrong tool, or the right tool with the wrong scope, because the prompt or context misframes what to do: for example, the production-database connector firing when test would do, or the email-send tool dispatching when the user only asked for a draft)
- skill supply-chain (the skill itself, or any skill the agent loads, came from somewhere - who authored it, who reviewed it, what it can do)

For each pattern, the lens produces one or two specific risks in the target system, ranked, with one suggested agent mitigation per risk - scope, split, filter, gate, or review. These sit on top of normal company controls (network controls, identity and access management, logging, vendor/security review), not in place of them. Name that explicitly in the lens's preamble.

Answer the agent's questions briefly, then hand back the rest: "You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."

Take stock of the packaged check

What happened:

Module 4's audit exercise loads the skill and runs it against the same system.

The point:

The policy files are source material. The skill carries the judgment about what matters in this system, with all four risk patterns as mandatory checks. Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them. The first loaded use should be the real audit.

Exercise

Exercise: Audit your agent

Time: 35 minutes. Phase 1 ~3, Phase 2 ~12, Phase 3 ~10, Phase 4 ~10.

Session (new, "Module 4 - Security audit")

Start a new session at your training-directory root. Your Exercise 1 skill is available in this project.

Name it m4-agent-audit if supported.

What you do:

Run your Exercise 1 security check against the system you built in modules 2-3. Add one mitigation and one residual-risk decision (what remains after mitigation). The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.

Bring the policy raw report (baseline), the check (expert), your Module 3 system (target).

Phase 1: Load the reusable check

3 min

Open this exercise in a fresh session at your training-directory root, after saving the Exercise 1 skill, so the session can find it.

Type / and look for /agent-audit in the autocomplete list. That means the skill is available. The audit prompts in the phases that follow tell it which of its two lenses to apply.

If /agent-audit doesn't appear, go back to Exercise 1, save the skill, then open a new session.

Phase 2: Run the policy audit

12 min

Ask the agent to apply the packaged policy lens to your full module-3 system and produce one report. Unlike the raw report from module-4/policies/, this one comes through the reusable lens you shaped.

If the audit doesn't fire, expand /agent-audit from the autocomplete in the prompt dialog.

Prompt (Cowork)


/agent-audit — load the skill



Apply the policy lens to the agent system: the memory in memory/, the sources in sources/, the agent files in agents/, the root CLAUDE.md, and the multi-agent runs in module-3/stances/.

For each rule the policy lens carries, produce one row in a report: rule name, one-line description, verdict (compliant / violating / "I can't tell"), and one line of evidence from my actual files for that verdict. If you can't tell, say what evidence you'd need to decide.

Write the packaged-lens report to outputs/policy-report.md. If outputs/policy-report-raw.md exists, briefly note one way the packaged report is sharper, narrower, or more specific than the raw run. Be specific. Be plain. An "I can't tell" is a better answer than a confident guess.

Read the memory and agent files properly - don't skim. Quote the specific lines or files that support each verdict.

After writing the report, read outputs/policy-report.md back to yourself and tell me:
1. The top three surprises - rows where the verdict is not what a careful reader would have predicted.
2. The three rows where "I can't tell" is most likely hiding a real compliance gap.
3. One row that looks compliant on the surface but where you would still push back.

Keep each point to one or two sentences. Quote the specific rule name so I can find the row.

Apply the policy lens to the agent system: the memory in memory/, the sources in sources/, the agent files in agents/, the root AGENTS.md, and the multi-agent runs in module-3/stances/.

For each rule the policy lens carries, produce one row in a report: rule name, one-line description, verdict (compliant / violating / "I can't tell"), and one line of evidence from my actual files for that verdict. If you can't tell, say what evidence you'd need to decide.

Write the packaged-lens report to outputs/policy-report.md. If outputs/policy-report-raw.md exists, briefly note one way the packaged report is sharper, narrower, or more specific than the raw run. Be specific. Be plain. An "I can't tell" is a better answer than a confident guess.

Read the memory and agent files properly - don't skim. Quote the specific lines or files that support each verdict.

After writing the report, read outputs/policy-report.md back to yourself and tell me:
1. The top three surprises - rows where the verdict is not what a careful reader would have predicted.
2. The three rows where "I can't tell" is most likely hiding a real compliance gap.
3. One row that looks compliant on the surface but where you would still push back.

Keep each point to one or two sentences. Quote the specific rule name so I can find the row.

Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.

Read the agent's three lists. Then open outputs/policy-report.md and find the rows it flagged.

Phase 3: Run the agent-risk audit

10 min

In the same session, ask the agent to apply the agent-security lens and write the ranked risk report.

Prompt (Cowork)

Apply the agent-security lens to every agent in agents/. Run both checks: what each agent can reach, and the named risk patterns the lens carries.

For access control: for each agent in agents/, list every outside system or sensitive place the agent can reach (connectors, retrievals, file writes beyond the training directory). Is each access necessary for what the agent actually does? Flag anything the agent has access to but doesn't need.

For the named risk patterns (prompt injection direct and indirect, secrets-in-context-and-scrollback, tool-confusion, skill supply-chain): for each pattern, name the top one or two specific risks across the agents, not generic definitions. Quote the agent file or behaviour that creates the risk.

For each risk flagged, suggest one mitigation for how the agent works - scope, split, filter, gate, or review - matched to the specific risk. These sit on top of the normal company controls already in place (network controls, identity and access management, logging, vendor/security review), not replacing them. Rank the risks by severity x likelihood, three-tier (high / medium / low).

Write the report to outputs/security-report.md. Include the ranked mitigation suggestions.

Prompt (Cowork)

Apply a mitigation to my system for the risk I'm about to name. Pick the shape from the five (scope, split, filter, gate, review), make the file or instruction changes, and walk me through what you did and why. If the shape doesn't fit, I'll tell you and we'll iterate.

Then re-run the check the reusable lens performed for this specific risk (re-apply the relevant lens, not the whole audit). Report the new verdict. Is the risk reduced, eliminated, or shifted somewhere else?

Then append a short section to outputs/security-report.md named "Mitigation applied and residual". Name what changed, what the new verdict is, and what's still true after the mitigation. Do not rewrite the earlier report. Not what we fixed. What's left. Be specific.
