Escalate to a person when judgment runs out

Still not sure? Ask a person.

Sometimes the right next step is not another prompt. If the policy report still has a serious "I can't tell", or the security report names a risk you do not know how to accept, show the evidence to someone who owns that area: legal, security, IT, compliance, or the business owner. Bring the report, the files it quotes, the mitigation you applied, and the residual that remains.

The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report. Walk in with that.

Separate prototype from production

Prototype vs production.

We did this for one risk. A production agent has a check or a closed door wherever its actions cannot be undone, and only a light check where redo is cheap. You must do the work.

Take stock of the loop you ran

What happened:

The Module 3 system has two packaged-lens reports and the earlier raw policy report. You applied one mitigation and recorded one residual decision in the security report. When judgment is unclear, show a human expert.

The point:

Certainty is not on offer. The discipline is the loop: assess, mitigate, reassess the residual, decide. The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent. The report carries the evidence and decisions.

This was Recipe 4: the two-lens audit, four agent-risk patterns, five mitigations (scope, split, filter, gate, review), and "I can't tell" as a verdict. For the next agent, the Cookbook for Agent System Design names the moves and components.

Lecture

Lecture: The discipline of risk

You built something that works. Would you bet your job on it being safe? Testing, policy and certification do not give agent systems certainty.

Classical security manages risk on predictable software

Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output. You find the bug, fix it, and check that the fix holds. That is why perimeter, access control and patching work.

Three ways agents break the old story

The behaviour is non-deterministic. Same prompt, same files, same tools, different session, different answer. One passing test is one sample.

The attack surface is the instruction set. Well-formed English in a document your agent reads can make it decide to do something harmful with access it has.

Capability is emergent. You can't fully predict the combination, only bound it.

The result: safe enough, under these conditions, within these limits, for now. What may the agent read? What may it change? What must come back to a human?

Assess, then mitigate

The work is a loop of four plain, repeatable steps.

Assess. Run your company's rules against your agent, then package that policy check to rerun. The agent-risk lens asks what the agent can reach, leak, and be misled into by ordinary text. Read the reports with judgment.

Mitigate. Pick one risk and apply the smallest change that reduces it: scope (give the agent less), split (two agents, different trust levels), filter (post-process output), gate (human approves) or review (a second agent judges).

Reassess the residual, then decide

Reassess the residual. Name the risk that remains and write it down: the residual risk is X; if Y happens, we made it less likely, not prevented it.

Decide. Accept the residual on record, or close the door.

"I can't tell" is a real answer. Closing it takes evidence, not a better guess.

The discipline is running the loop, not reaching certainty.

Now the move is to give it less

You have given the agent more: context, memory, more stances. Now give it less.

More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.

Every door you close is a source the agent won't read; every tool you remove is a capability gone. Scope it down far enough and the system is safe and useless. You pick it, write down what is left, and sign for it.

The best mitigation is the door you don't open

The cheapest, most reliable way to reduce risk on an agent is to not open the door in the first place.

Should the agent have write access to that system? If not, scope down before you scope up. Should the agent read from that mailbox? If not, don't connect it. Should the agent draft customer-facing language? If that is where the biggest risk lives, a human drafts and the agent reviews.

Every door you don't open is a residual risk you don't have to name, mitigate or re-test.

Expect it to cost you a feature. It costs whoever sells you agents too, this training included: an agent that reaches less is a smaller thing to sell, and it is still the right call.

The discipline is what carries

Some of your agents will be wrong in ways you won't catch. The organisations that handle this well run the loop openly, name residual risks plainly, and close doors they don't need to open. Damn, this is complex stuff.

Read the reports. Pick a risk. Apply a mitigation. Name what's left. Decide.

Debrief

Five minutes. The agent reviews the policy and security reports, writes a rule only where no check or mitigation stands, and cuts any earlier rule your mitigation now covers.

Prompt (Cowork)

Start by reading the files. No plan or preamble.

Review this session and compound 1-5 security operating rules into the agent system. Read the root ./CLAUDE.md if it exists. Read outputs/policy-report-raw.md if it exists, outputs/policy-report.md, and outputs/security-report.md. Look back over the session: which rows should future sessions remember, which "I can't tell" rows need standing evidence checks, where did the mitigation reduce one risk but shift another, and what residuals should future sessions not forget?

Be harsher than feels right. Security rules that sound generally wise but do not name a concrete trigger, file, report row, or residual do not count.

Then update ./CLAUDE.md as the durable operating memory for this agent system. Add or sharpen 1-5 short security rules only where no check or mitigation can stand (what not to touch, which residuals from outputs/security-report.md must stay visible), and cut any earlier rule that your mitigation or the reusable security check now covers. Integrate them into the right section if one exists; otherwise create a short section named "Security operating rules". Do not edit the skill files. Do not paste an audit summary. Do not add a retro section. Do not remove or restructure any existing sections outside Security operating rules. Each rule should be usable by a future agent that never saw this session.

When you're done, read back the Security operating rules section and copy the exact rule text you changed or added. Then tell me in 1-5 lines: which report row or residual drove each rule, what future agents must do differently, and what risk remains even after the mitigation.

Point the check at the other agents you've built.

Build More Skills For Recurring How

A skill packages the how of a recurring judgment or workflow, so the agent repeats the method without you rebuilding it. Other examples: reviewing customer data use, preparing a weekly briefing, triaging a queue.

A skill works across projects and agents. Sharpen it where the method proves thin.

To share, install the skill in a teammate's runtime. Their agent loads the same method by name, without your prompt history. A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.

Key Concepts

  • No certainty: assess, mitigate, reassess the residual, decide.
  • Anything the agent reads can instruct it, a source included.
  • "I can't tell" is a real answer.
  • Mitigations add to security controls, never replace them.

Bring to Module 5

Write one sentence per case: "the missing organisational check was X." Both cases are in the pre-reads that follow.

Pre-reads before Module 5

Read Mata v. Avianca (2023) and the Deloitte Australia / DEWR report (2025) in the lecture.

Lecture

The Missing Check

What you do:

Read two public cases. In each, a court or a government record documents what the LLM produced and which organisational check was missing.

In both cases the truth was one lookup away. The LLM filled the gap with something plausible, and no step in the workflow opened the source.

Case 1: Mata v. Avianca (S.D.N.Y., 2023)

A passenger's attorneys filed a brief that cited six cases. None of them existed. One attorney had found them with ChatGPT, then asked ChatGPT whether one of them was real. It said yes. Nobody checked a legal research database.

On June 22, 2023, Judge P. Kevin Castel fined both attorneys and their firm $5,000. The order blames the missing verification, not the tool.

Read:

  • The sanctions opinion itself (readable, and it quotes Schwartz's affidavit directly): law.justia.com, Mata v. Avianca, Opinion and Order of June 22, 2023
  • CNBC's contemporaneous coverage for the shape of it: CNBC, Judge sanctions lawyers whose AI-written filing contained fake citations

Case 2: Deloitte Australia / DEWR report (2025)

Australia's employment department paid Deloitte A$439,000 for a review. Academic Dr. Christopher Rudge found references that did not exist and a quote falsely attributed to a judge.

The 3 October 2025 revision disclosed GPT-4o use, including for completing citations. Deloitte refunded the final installment. Rudge found new false references in the revision. The department replaced the report again on 3 February 2026.

Read:

  • The department's current report page and correction history: DEWR, Targeted Compliance Framework Assurance Review – Final Report
  • The released correspondence describing the approved toolchain, publishing uses, review, and missed errors: Department of Finance, FOI 25-26-084 Document 1
  • The Guardian's account, including Rudge's findings and the refund: Guardian, Deloitte to pay money back to Albanese government after using AI in A$440,000 report
  • The Register's technical summary, including the GPT-4o disclosure and the "new fake refs in the revision" detail: The Register, Deloitte to refund part of A$440k Australian report after AI snafu

Why the LLM fabricates

  • It completes the pattern. An LLM continues text in the form that looks right. A legal brief or consulting report calls for case names and citations, so they arrive whether or not the fact exists.
  • It fills gaps instead of stopping. When the sources miss a piece, the model supplies what makes the answer feel complete.
  • It verifies inside the same fiction. Asking the same model "are you sure?" is another fluent answer, not a check on the world. Verification has to leave the session and touch the source.
  • It inherits organisational shortcuts. If the workflow rewards speed and has no step where someone opens the cited source, the fabrication survives.

Why grounding fails even when the facts are in context

  • The source is present but does no work. Buried under drafts and notes, a source sits beside a claim without supporting it. The LLM answers from the pattern the topic evokes.
  • The source says less than the answer. A file says one customer complained; the answer says customers are unhappy.
  • Conflict gets smoothed. Two sources disagree, and the LLM writes a clean synthesis. Grounded work keeps the disagreement visible.

Bring to Module 5

One sentence per case: "The organisational check that would have caught this was X."

Once the files are saved to disk, end this session. Module 5 starts fresh at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Can you trust what the agent says inside its scope?

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Catching Hallucinations

Big Idea

There is truth out there, and your agent's job is to stay connected to it. Where it cannot reach a source, it fills the gap: confident, plausible, wrong. Grounding, and checks you test on your own output, make the gap visible.

Prework

Read The Missing Check: two public-record cases with documented organisational root causes.

Write one sentence per case: "the missing organisational check was X."

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Detect hallucinations
  • Benchmark AI checks
  • Build a judge

Start here

Session (new, "Module 5 - Catching hallucinations")

Working folder: ~/Documents/agents-101/.

The question, to you: which line in your Module 3 briefing reads almost right? Point at it.

Lecture

Lecture: Grounded, and four candidates to measure

There is truth out there

There is truth out there. Your sources carry shards of it. The LLM, left to itself, has no model of truth, only a model of what usually comes next in language that looks like yours.

When your sources support a request, the output is grounded. When they don't, the agent still produces something, and the tone looks the same.

Grounded means traceable to a specific file, number or quote in a source. A grounded claim can still be wrong if its source is wrong. Start with grounded.

Mostly right, ten times over, is mostly wrong

If an agent is 85% correct on a single step (an illustrative number), that sounds forgivable.

Ten unverified steps in a row (retrieval, synthesis, formatting, writing, checking, rewriting, summarising, publishing) at 85% each come to about 20% end-to-end: one task in five correct, four in five with a defect, usually where you won't see it.

A short loop (look up the order, check the policy, draft the reply) stacks little. A full workflow with no check compounds every miss.

The number doesn't tell you what will go wrong, only that something will. Design for that.

A test-and-fix loop collapses the error rate

Say your briefing is 10% fabricated, and a detector catches 90% of those claims. Fix what it flags, then test again.

Round 1: 10% → 1%. Round 2: 1% → 0.1%. Round 3: 0.1% → 0.01%.

The numbers are illustrative. They show that compounding breaks a single pass but helps you once each round checks against the sources.

"Are you sure?" is another fluent answer

When you can't tell whether an answer is grounded, asking the agent "Are you sure?" returns another answer from the same source, in the same confident voice.

Large language models generate the next likely word, not the next true one. They are trained on confident, specific, fluent text, so they produce language that looks like that whether or not the material supports it. Fluency is not evidence, and the model cannot tell you which parts of its output are grounded.

Later models may fabricate less; the mechanism stays the same.

Steering without reading every line

I stopped reading full documents at work some time ago. I read to steer on a high level. Much of the text is for the LLM itself.

Grounding is what makes that safe. A line on my CV is a claim. You would check it against my work contract, not my LinkedIn profile. A check that goes to the ground lets you steer text you do not read.

Don't pick a method. Run the candidates.

Every grounding check misses something. Advice won't tell you what it misses on your material.

Run several checks in parallel on your own output. Four agents check the same 30 claims. A scorer measures each one for precision, recall and coverage.

Four candidates that fail differently

Each method tests a different link between a claim and its source.

1. Source triangulation. Does the claim appear in at least one source file? Catches invention.

2. Entailment. Do the sources support everything the claim says? Catches overreach.

3. Citation integrity. Does the cited source contain the claim? Catches citations that point at nothing.

4. Counter-evidence search. Does any source contradict the claim? Catches claims that fail when someone tests them against the evidence.

You have done this before

On the Mata v. Avianca pre-read, each method found a different gap:

  • Source triangulation: an unsourced "small firm" and an unsupported "ten minutes" estimate.
  • Entailment: a too-clean Schwartz timeline.
  • Citation integrity: a quote absent from the sanctions order.
  • Counter-evidence: CNBC blurring the $5,000 sanction.

The judge names its own limit

The winner, or the top two together, becomes a reusable judge file. The file names the method, why it won, and what it misses.

A groundedness judge catches invented content. It does not catch a wrong source, framing that tilts, what was left out, or a strategic call.

Check the text before it becomes an action

An agent action starts as text: a mail, a ticket update, a CRM change. Unsupported text becomes an unsupported action.

Have the agent propose. Check the proposal against sources or a judge. Then apply.

A drift signal, never proof

Run the same briefing prompt twice from the same sources, in two sessions. Compare what stays and what changes.

A stable claim can still be unsupported. Drift is a warning, not proof of fabrication. Two sessions give you a demo; the signal firms up at five to ten.

Exercise

Exercise: Hallucination benchmark

Time: 55 minutes. Phase 1 ~8, Phase 2 ~8, Phase 3 ~20, Phase 4 ~10, Phase 5 close ~9.

Session (new, "Module 5 - Hallucination benchmark")

What you do:

You set up a benchmark: a 30-claim pool, four detection methods, and a scorer that checks each claim against the evidence. Run all four on your own output and keep the one that scores best, or the ensemble if it does. The winner becomes a judge file.

Phase 2: Run the four detectors

8 min

Four helper agents run in parallel on the same claim pool, each with its own detection method and output file.

In your main session:

Prompt (Claude Code Desktop)

Run four detectors on `module-5/claim-pool.md` in parallel. Each detector is a subagent with a different method. Each reads `module-5/claim-pool.md`, `module-5/briefing.md`, `module-5/evidence-roster.md`, and the rostered evidence files named there. Each writes its findings as a list of claim-pool claims flagged, with one line of reasoning per claim.

Detector 1 — Source triangulation. For every claim in the claim pool, check whether that claim appears in at least one file on disk. If no file supports it, flag it UNGROUNDED. Write to `module-5/detectors/source-triangulation.md`.

Detector 2 — Entailment. For every claim in the claim pool, ask: does the briefing say more than the sources actually support? A source that says "one customer complained" doesn't support "the market is unhappy." Flag OVERREACH when the briefing stretches what the source said. Write to `module-5/detectors/entailment.md`.

Detector 3 — Citation integrity. Some claims in the claim pool will cite a source, either inline or implicitly. For each citation, open the cited file and check whether the file actually contains the specific claim attributed to it. Flag CITATION-BROKEN when the citation doesn't back the claim. Write to `module-5/detectors/citation-integrity.md`.

Detector 4 — Counter-evidence search. For every claim in the claim pool, actively look for evidence that contradicts it, not just evidence that supports it. Flag CRUMBLES when disconfirming material exists in the rostered evidence that the briefing ignored. Write to `module-5/detectors/counter-evidence.md`.

One rule across all four detectors: quote each flagged claim exactly as it appears in `module-5/claim-pool.md`. The scorer uses strict substring match; paraphrased findings count as misses.

Spawn all four in parallel. When they finish, confirm that these four files exist: `module-5/detectors/source-triangulation.md`, `module-5/detectors/entailment.md`, `module-5/detectors/citation-integrity.md`, and `module-5/detectors/counter-evidence.md`.

Phase 3: Scorer runs the benchmark

20 min

A fifth agent, the scorer, scores the four detector files against the 30 claims:

  • precision: of what the detector flagged, how much was ungrounded?
  • recall: of the ungrounded claims, how many did the detector catch?
  • coverage: did the detector look at the claim pool?

Prompt (Cowork)

You are the scorer for a four-way detector benchmark. Your inputs:

- Claim pool: `module-5/claim-pool.md`
- Briefing: `module-5/briefing.md`
- Evidence roster: `module-5/evidence-roster.md` and the rostered evidence files named there
- Detector output 1: `module-5/detectors/source-triangulation.md`
- Detector output 2: `module-5/detectors/entailment.md`
- Detector output 3: `module-5/detectors/citation-integrity.md`
- Detector output 4: `module-5/detectors/counter-evidence.md`

Your job: adjudicate the 30 claims, score each detector against that adjudication, produce a scoreboard, name a winner.

First, create the reference adjudication. For every claim in `module-5/claim-pool.md`, label it GROUNDED, UNGROUNDED, or PARTLY GROUNDED. Quote the evidence line or file that supports the label. If you cannot find support in the rostered evidence, say so plainly. Save this reference set to `module-5/adjudicated-claims.md`.

For each detector:
1. Match detector findings to claim-pool claims by strict substring match. If you can't find the exact claim-pool phrase in the detector's output, count as MISS. Do not reason about semantic similarity, do not paraphrase-match, do not accept "close enough."
2. For each claim, check whether the detector flagged it. If the adjudication says UNGROUNDED or PARTLY GROUNDED, the detector should have flagged it. Count that as a hit. If the adjudication says GROUNDED, the detector should not have flagged it. Count that as a false positive.
3. Compute precision (hits / total flagged) and recall (hits / total claims adjudicated UNGROUNDED or PARTLY GROUNDED). Coverage = how many of the 30 claim-pool claims the detector looked at.
4. One line of qualitative notes — what this detector caught that others missed, what it missed, where its method is strong, where it's weak.

Save the scoreboard to module-5/scoreboard.md as a table:

| Detector | Precision | Recall | Coverage | Hits | False positives | Misses | Notes |

After the table, name ONE winner. Do not return "all four are useful" — force the pick. If top two are within 10% precision and 10% recall of each other, name the single winner first, THEN propose a two-method ensemble and say what each catches that the other doesn't. Maximum ensemble cap: two methods. Never three.

At the bottom, add a one-line recommendation naming the detector or ensemble and the reason it won for output of this shape.

If `module-5/my-marks.md` exists, replace each `judge: -` there with your adjudication label, and add one line under the scoreboard table: on how many of those claims your adjudication agrees with my mark, and which ones differ.

Show me the full scoreboard table in chat after saving the file.

Phase 4: Save the winner as a judge

10 min

Keep the winner, or the two-method ensemble. Save it as a judge file: a named, reusable prompt you can run against any briefing.

Prompt (Cowork)

Take the winning detector (or the ensemble) from module-5/scoreboard.md. Rewrite it as a portable judge prompt. The judge should:

1. Take any output file and the relevant evidence files as inputs.
2. Flag ungrounded claims using the method(s) that won the benchmark.
3. Return a short structured list — claim flagged, category, one-line reasoning.
4. Not classify claims I didn't ask about. Stay narrow. A judge that tries to do everything does nothing well.

Write the judge as a markdown file to judges/groundedness-judge.md — a short heading, one paragraph describing what it checks and why, then the prompt itself (the thing I'd paste into the agent to run the judge). Keep the judge prompt under 20 lines. Prompts that sprawl get ignored.

At the end of the file, add a one-line "Known limit:" — the failure mode this judge doesn't catch, based on what lost the benchmark.

Carry the benchmark pattern forward

The point:

You pick a quality check by running candidates on your own output and scoring them against your own reference. The winner becomes a judge you can defend. The pattern (candidates → benchmark → scorer → winner) works for any quality judgment you automate.

This was Recipe 5. The Cookbook for Agent System Design holds the moves and components.

Debrief

Five minutes. The agent reviews the benchmark, points future sessions at the saved judge, writes a rule only where the judge cannot check, and cuts any earlier rule the judge covers.

Prompt (Cowork)

Start by reading the files. No plan or preamble.

Review this session and update the root `./CLAUDE.md` with groundedness operating rules. Read `./CLAUDE.md` if it exists, then scan `module-5/evidence-roster.md`, `module-5/claim-pool.md`, `module-5/adjudicated-claims.md`, `module-5/detectors/` (the four detector outputs), `module-5/scoreboard.md`, and `judges/groundedness-judge.md`.

Look back over the session: when did ungroundedness matter, which claim-shapes needed checking, where did citations look present but not load-bearing, and what should future agents know before they turn a briefing, memo, recommendation, or proposed action into something people rely on?

Then update `./CLAUDE.md` as the durable operating memory for this agent system. Add or sharpen 1-4 short rules that name where `judges/groundedness-judge.md` runs and where the benchmark showed it cannot check, and tell future sessions to answer "not enough evidence" there instead of smoothing over the gap; quote one earlier rule the judge now covers and cut it, or say none exists. If a Groundedness checks section already exists, edit the rules in that section in place; do not add a new subheading or parallel list. Otherwise create a short section named "Groundedness checks". Touch ONLY that section; preserve every other section verbatim. Do not paste a benchmark summary. Do not add a retro section. Each rule should be usable by a future agent that never saw this session.

When you're done, read back the Groundedness checks section you just wrote and confirm each rule is in the file. Copy the exact rule text, one line per rule. Then tell me in 1-5 lines: what changed in `./CLAUDE.md`, which scoreboard row or adjudicated claim drove it, what future agents must do differently, and which claim shape you are LEAST confident you caught correctly. Then name the two patterns this prompt enforced: one about which boundary you were allowed to touch, one about checking what landed after you wrote it.

Notice what the prompt insists on

The prompt names the boundary: touch only the Groundedness checks section, keep every other section verbatim. Without it, a small edit becomes a rewrite and earlier rules drift.

The prompt also makes the agent re-read the section and confirm each rule is there. The agent's report says what it intended, the file says what happened.

Push back on the summary

Correct the agent where a rule is vague: "name the evidence roster", "say when to stop and ask for sources."

Start with the costly, repeatable misses: numbers in external notes, customer names in account summaries, policy claims in internal advice, citations in briefings. Put the trigger in the root instructions file.

Propose, double-check, apply

An agent action starts as text: a mail, a ticket update, a CRM change. Wrong text becomes a wrong action.

For actions that matter, the agent proposes, the judge or a lookup in the source checks the proposal, and the agent applies only what passes.

Which check would let this action go without you?

Read What is an Agent, The autonomy ladder before you decide what the agent may do next.

A judge you have tested clears what can be redone; where an action cannot be undone, the expert also reviews the proposal, its evidence, and the judge's known limit.

Key Concepts

  • Grounded means traceable to a specific file, number or quote. Where the sources end, the agent keeps writing in the same voice.
  • Asking the agent "are you sure?" returns another fluent answer. A check has to touch the source.
  • The agent runs candidate detectors on your own output; you read the scoreboard and keep the winner.
  • The judge passed one benchmark. It names its own limit: wrong sources, framing and strategic choices stay outside it.
  • Reusable pattern: candidates, benchmark, scorer, winner.

Pre-reads before Module 6

Ethan Mollick, "Garbage Can and Bitter Lesson."

End this session once the judge is saved. Module 6 starts fresh in ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Next

You can spot ungrounded output with a judge. Next, the judge goes into a loop, and the work improves under its feedback without you at the keyboard.

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Evaluations

Big Idea

Put the Module 5 judge in a loop and the work improves by itself. The generator sharpens against the judge's feedback, round after round, while you walk away.

Prework

Ethan Mollick, The Bitter Lesson versus The Garbage Can. Start with the judge you saved at the close of Module 5.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Run an eval loop
  • Steer agents with feedback

Start here

Start a fresh session or task at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Read Ethan Mollick's The Bitter Lesson versus The Garbage Can.

His question: will the bitter lesson apply inside your company? Can agents improve if you define the outcome and let them find the path, or does organisational mess still matter too much?

Run the loop without you in it

The same judge keeps catching what slipped past, and the system absorbs the catches without your edits.

Lecture

Evals as Steering

Ethan Mollick's The Bitter Lesson versus The Garbage Can asks a question. The bitter lesson may apply to companies: define the outcome, give the agent examples and feedback, and let it find its own path. Or the garbage can wins, and the path carries the organisation.

You can stay inside one loop. You cannot stay inside all of them. Evals write down what good means so the system keeps applying it when you are not in the chair.

Evals turn checks into a loop: the model generates, the judge checks, the tactic changes, the next session starts sharper.

Module 5 turned judgment into a judge

One briefing, thirty claims, four detectors, one scorer: the scoreboard named which method caught the misses. The winner is saved as judges/groundedness-judge.md, measured judgment made runnable. That is the first kind of eval.

Groundedness protects the floor

A groundedness eval protects the floor: every name appears in the source, every number traces to a file, every claim cites evidence or admits the gap.

Not enough.

Steering raises the ceiling

Two mails both avoid overclaiming; one is forgettable, the other makes the reader act.

Perhaps it names the tradeoff and gives a clean next move.

Define that dimension as a check. That is a steering eval: did the output overperform on it?

Groundedness protects the floor. Steering raises the ceiling.

A grounded mail can still be useless, so you need both.

Three rounds, nobody editing

The Module 5 judge goes into a loop.

Round 1 produces a briefing. The judge scores it and writes per-claim feedback. The main session rewrites ./generation-tactic.md from the feedback. Rounds 2 and 3 run with the sharper tactic, and the score rises with nobody editing.

Walk away. On return, the notes show each round's score and what changed. The judge stayed fixed, so the rise is the work getting better.

The answer is never "the eval passed"

What would have to be true for this eval to be the right one?

The eval checks the thing that matters, at the moment where the mistake would hurt, against a standard you would defend. You decide which details the system must never miss.

The same pattern applies to actions. An agent action starts as text: a proposed mail, ticket update, CRM change or command. Check the proposal before it becomes the action.

Exercise

Exercise: The eval loop runs itself

Time: 45 min: manual run ~5, walk-away ~30, return and read notes ~10.

Session (new, "Module 6 - Evaluations")

What you do:

Watch your Module 3 briefing get better round after round, with nobody editing it.

Eval as infrastructure: a generator writes a briefing from its tactic, the judge scores it with per-claim feedback, and the main session rewrites the tactic. The judge stays fixed, so a rising score is the work getting better. Run at least three rounds, then continue until improvement stops.

Helper agents are isolated workers, each with fresh context for its own job.

Example run note: round 0, the Module 3 briefing, flagged 11 claims; round 1 flagged 7, round 2 flagged 7, round 3 flagged 4.

Phase 1: Score your Module 3 briefing

5 min

Ask the agent to score your Module 3 briefing with the judge from Module 5, then write the first generation tactic from what the judge flagged.

Prompt (Cowork)

Three things, in sequence:

1. Dispatch a judge subagent, as the loop will. It reads judges/groundedness-judge.md, ./crux.md without its ## Answer section, memory/, and the ## Answer section of module-3/briefing-baseline.md, your Module 3 briefing as you froze it, and nothing else. It writes module-6/runs/round-0/judgment.md, with claims judged and claims flagged on the top line.

2. If module-5/baseline-score.md exists, put its "Claims judged: N. Claims flagged: F." line beside today's count. Any difference on the same briefing is a first read of the judge's own noise; say how big it is.

3. Write ./generation-tactic.md from that judgment, as the generator instruction: produce a fresh one-page briefing on the question in ./crux.md, from ./crux.md without its ## Answer section and from memory/. One rule for each kind of miss the judge flagged, each rule naming the miss it prevents. Keep it short enough that a generator will follow it.

Then tell me in five lines: claims judged and flagged in the Module 3 briefing, the Module 5 count beside it, whether the line I doubted in Module 3 was flagged, the rule the judgment most clearly asks for, and one claim the judge could not check from the files.

Phase 2: Start the loop, then walk away

30 min

Generation and judging run in separate helpers; the lead reads the judgment and rewrites ./generation-tactic.md between rounds.

Prompt (Cowork)

Run an eval loop using my fixed judge.

Fixed judge:
- Never edit judges/groundedness-judge.md.
- Before round 1, compute and record the starting SHA of judges/groundedness-judge.md.
- When the loop stops, compute the ending SHA and report whether the judge stayed byte-identical.

Starting generation tactic:
- Read ./generation-tactic.md and module-6/runs/round-0/judgment.md from round 0. If either is missing, stop and tell me round 0 has not run.
- Create module-6/runs/round-1/, module-6/runs/round-2/, and module-6/runs/round-3/. If the loop continues, keep the same numbering pattern with round-4/, round-5/, and so on.

Run at least 3 rounds. After round 3, keep going until there is no longer significant improvement from the previous round.

For each round:
1. Dispatch a generator subagent. It must read ./generation-tactic.md, ./crux.md without its ## Answer section, and memory/. It writes the briefing for that round:
   - briefing.md in that round's folder
2. Dispatch a separate judge subagent. It must read judges/groundedness-judge.md, ./crux.md without its ## Answer section, memory/, and the briefing for that round, and nothing else. Give it no extra rules, checks or instructions beyond the judge file. It writes the judgment for that round:
   - judgment.md in that round's folder
   Each judgment includes verdicts, one-sentence grounding feedback per factual claim, one generation-tactic rule for each flagged failure class, plus a top-line count of flagged claims.
3. The main session, not a subagent, reads the judgment for that round and any new lines in ./remarks.md, and rewrites ./generation-tactic.md for the next round. Integrate the lesson; do not append retro notes. Remarks are my reading as the person receiving the briefing; they go into the tactic only, never to the judge. With no remarks, the loop runs the same.
4. Starting after round 3, decide whether the last round improved significantly compared with the previous round. Significant improvement means a drop in flagged claims larger than the judge noise read in round 0, a new failure class resolved, or a clearly sharper generation tactic. When there is no longer significant improvement, stop the loop.

When the loop stops:
- Write module-6/eval-notes.md with a table of claims flagged out of claims judged, round 0 (the Module 3 briefing) first and then each loop round, the generation-tactic change after each round, naming any remark it came from, why the loop stopped, the judge SHA check, whether any judge subagent got instructions beyond the judge file, one thing the judge still cannot see, and one human decision still needed.
- In chat, show me the same summary in under 12 lines.

Do not stop for confirmation between rounds.

No preamble. Start by computing and recording the judge's starting SHA, then run round 1.

Use these inputs; no preamble, start by writing the first generation tactic file:
Lecture

When the score stops moving

When flagged claims drop toward zero and stay there, the judge has stopped finding things. That does not mean the work is done.

A flat score is information about the judge or the work

A flat score is information about the judge or the work. Check both. The judge measures one thing: whether claims stay tied to the evidence. A grounded claim can still be vague or obvious, and this judge passes it.

Sharper framing, a recommendation that commits, a briefing someone reads to the end: the judge cannot see these. When the number stops moving, your judgment comes back in.

You haven't checked the judge yet

You marked claims against the judge in Module 5. Do that once for every judge you intend to trust: where it passed something you would have sent back, you agree less often than the number suggests.

If the model stops fabricating, what is your judge for?

Your judge catches claims that float free of the evidence. Every model release makes that check cheaper. No release so far has told anyone what good means in your company.

The rest is yours to name.

Lecture

The New Human Role in the Loop

Files are the handles. Connectors bring material in. Agents read and write. Judges hold a line. Loops make the next session sharper.

The destination is not "the human disappears." You move one level up: you design the loop and own the yardstick.

Which check would let it send the mail without you?

Would you allow your agent to send an internal mail related to what you do: a project update, a decision summary, a risk note, a stakeholder nudge?

What would have to be true before you let the agent hit send?

  • Sounds like it came from your world (Module 1).
  • The sources, current facts and open questions (Module 2).
  • The right searches and stances before it writes (Module 3).
  • Boundaries: what it can read, what it never says, which risks it can't tell (Module 4).
  • A groundedness judge ties names, numbers, claims and recommendations to evidence (Module 5).

Variety in, selection out, memory keeps

Something makes several candidates, something else picks, and what wins gets written down. The three stances and four detectors are the generating half. The floor and ceiling evals are the picking half.

While you are away, the generator makes more than you need, the judge discards most of it, and the tactic file keeps what survived.

The human moves one level up

The old role sits between agent and world: the agent drafts, you inspect. That does not work for a system.

The new role is to design the loop: what the agent can reach, what it writes down, what stays fixed, what may change, what gets checked every time, what "better" means, where the human still belongs.

The answer may be draft only, review first, send to yourself first, or automatic when the groundedness judge passes and the goal-nudger scores high. Some categories never go without a human.

Make the goal-nudger

Create one steering eval for internal mail an agent could help with. Ask the agent to build it with you:

Prompt (Cowork)

Help me create a steering eval for internal mail I might let an agent draft or send.

The eval is not a groundedness check. Assume groundedness is handled by `judges/groundedness-judge.md`. This eval should create positive pressure to overperform on one dimension that matters for my work.

Ask me at most three questions at a time, wait for my answers, and do not show a longer hidden list. For each round, recommend the answer you infer from my context so I can accept or correct it. Stop after two rounds: if the dimension is still not judgeable, propose the narrowest observable version and mark the remaining uncertainty. Start by offering examples I can choose from or adapt:

- executive crispness
- commercial sharpness
- specificity
- risk awareness
- actionability
- reader empathy
- strategic usefulness
- sounds like our team

If I choose a vague word, use the remaining question rounds to make it observable. For example, "strategic usefulness" might become: names the tradeoff, states a point of view, and gives the decision-maker a next move.

Once the dimension is clear, show me:

1. The dimension name.
2. A one-sentence definition.
3. Three examples: a 5/5 mail excerpt, a 3/5 mail excerpt, and a 1/5 mail excerpt.
4. The scoring rubric from 1 to 5.
5. What the eval should ask the agent to improve when the score is 3 or lower.

Then save the eval as `./goal-nudger-eval.md`. Show me what you wrote and ask for one final correction before saving.

5. What the eval should ask the agent to improve when the score is 3 or lower.

Then save the eval as `./goal-nudger-eval.md`. Show me what you wrote and ask for one final correction before saving.

Prompt (Codex CLI)

Help me create a steering eval for internal mail I might let an agent draft or send.

The eval is not a groundedness check. Assume groundedness is handled by `judges/groundedness-judge.md`. This eval should create positive pressure to overperform on one dimension that matters for my work.

Ask me at most three questions at a time, wait for my answers, and do not show a longer hidden list. For each round, recommend the answer you infer from my context so I can accept or correct it. Stop after two rounds: if the dimension is still not judgeable, propose the narrowest observable version and mark the remaining uncertainty. Start by offering examples I can choose from or adapt:

- executive crispness
- commercial sharpness
- specificity
- risk awareness
- actionability
- reader empathy
- strategic usefulness
- sounds like our team

If I choose a vague word, use the remaining question rounds to make it observable. For example, "strategic usefulness" might become: names the tradeoff, states a point of view, and gives the decision-maker a next move.

Once the dimension is clear, show me:

1. The dimension name.
2. A one-sentence definition.
3. Three examples: a 5/5 mail excerpt, a 3/5 mail excerpt, and a 1/5 mail excerpt.
4. The scoring rubric from 1 to 5.
5. What the eval should ask the agent to improve when the score is 3 or lower.

Then save the eval as `./goal-nudger-eval.md`. Show me what you wrote and ask for one final correction before saving.

I drifted too

When I built a module of this course with an agent, the rules sat in its context the whole time. In one session: five reversals from me on the agent's confident recommendations, four leaks of a banned word across three helper agents, and several times a "done" that was not done.

A check loop caught what the helpers missed. I caught what the loop missed. That is why the loop still has a person in it.

The better it gets, the less you watch

Every clean week is evidence the loop works, and each one erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops. Design the loop and never run one yourself, and you lose the eye that made you worth putting in charge of it.

When did you last read one yourself?

This check has no instrument, only a date: when did you last read one of these start to finish, without the agent summarising it first?

If the answer is a month, put one in your calendar. Read one piece of the work the loop produced, the way the person receiving it will.

The full picture, and what it is made of

The full picture: model, context, tools, goal, loop, checks, boundary, interface. Each was one decision about what you give the agent and what you keep back.

Your role in the loop is to design the conditions for giving the system more autonomy, one loop at a time.

Debrief

Five minutes. The agent reads the round-by-round trail, sharpens the generator's tactic file in place and points your root instructions at it, so every briefing you ask for from now on is written from that tactic and checked by the same judge. The judge file stays untouched.

Prompt (Cowork)

Start by reading the files. No plan or preamble.

Review this session and sharpen the generator's tactic beyond what the loop reached. Read ./generation-tactic.md in its current state, then scan module-6/runs/ and module-6/eval-notes.md. The judge file at judges/groundedness-judge.md did not move; that is the integrity of the loop. Check that no judge subagent got rules beyond that file. If the flag counts stayed in single digits, say whether the changes between rounds are bigger than noise before crediting any tactic change. Then look back over the session: which tactic change helped, which one did not help and should be removed or rewritten, what specific boundary case did the loop never test, where did the generator keep missing the same thing across multiple rounds, and what did the judge flag that the tactic never absorbed?

Be harsher than feels comfortable. If a rule is vague, say so by name. If a rule fired on the wrong thing, name what it fired on.

Then overwrite ./generation-tactic.md in place. Do not create a new version. Integrate, don't append. Add the tactic rule the loop never reached, sharpen a rule that stayed too vague, remove the rule module-6/eval-notes.md names as the rule to cut, or say why it stays, and remove a rule that fired on the wrong thing. A removal means the rule is gone from the file, not renamed or scoped; if you scoped it instead, say so and why. The tactic file is infrastructure now. Every rule should name the failure class it pre-empts. Don't add a "retro notes" section; rewrite the file as the better version.

Last, add one line to the root instructions file: every briefing asked for in this folder is written from ./generation-tactic.md and scored by judges/groundedness-judge.md before it reaches me. If such a line exists, keep it as one line.

When you're done, tell me in 3-5 lines: what you added, what you sharpened, what you removed, and why, grounded in specific rounds. Name one boundary case the next run should test.

Push back on the summary

Read the agent's summary and push back: "That rule is too vague, make it observable" / "you added a rule the tactic already had after round 2."

If it sounds too kind, ask: "Which rule did you claim to remove but keep under another name? Quote both lines."

The artifact: the sharpened ./generation-tactic.md, the line in your root instructions that sends every later briefing through it, and one line in the Module 6 eval-notes naming the first always-on eval you'll run next.

Key Concepts

  • The loop improves the output round after round with nobody editing; the fixed judge is why the rise is real.
  • Groundedness protects the floor; steering raises the ceiling.
  • A flat score is information about the judge or the work. Check both.
  • You design the loop and own the yardstick.

Bring to Module 7

Your first five agent calls at work, written down, using Agent Trigger List. Pick one call the eval loop's checks could let run without you, and write the trigger into module-6/trigger.md.

The Cookbook for Agent System Design and What is an Agent are optional references.

Once the trigger is written, end this module's session or task. Module 7 starts fresh at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Next

Your system now improves its own output. Next, it starts working for someone besides you.

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

From Personal to Team

Big Idea

You can't really share an agent. You can share the context, a skill, the output, or an interface, and choosing between them is a strategy decision.

Prework

Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it. A licence rollout, a portal, or a shared drive works.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Share agent work with a team
  • Interview for the job to be done
  • Plan adoption

Start here

What would you want a teammate to have: your memory/ folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack? And why that one?

The agent writes the sharing plan into module-7/. module-7/monday.md holds the next move: one person, one question, one test.

Exercise

Exercise: Interview for the job and pick a candidate

Time: 25 minutes. 10 for the handover, 15 for the interview and the pick.

Session (new, "Module 7 - Personal to team")

Start with the teammate's work, not with "what should I share with my teammate?" What decides whether sharing works is the job your teammate is trying to get done. This is the Jobs-to-be-Done frame from Clayton Christensen and collaborators. Your agent, skill, output or interface is a candidate: does it do the job better than what they use today?

Hand your agent to a neighbour

10 min

Pair up. Copy two files into your neighbour's handover-in/ folder: the agent-audit skill from Module 4, and your Module 2 agent from agents/. Do not edit either. Only those files travel. Your memory/ and sources/ stay with you.

Your neighbour pastes this prompt. Their agent runs both files on their own system and writes a report for you.

Prompt (Cowork)

My neighbour handed me two files: a skill and an agent's instructions. They are in handover-in/. Their memory and sources stayed with them.

Run both on my system, on a real piece of my own work. Do not fix either file first.

Then write the report my neighbour gets back. Use exactly these headings:

## Received
The two file paths and the coding agent you ran them in.

## Skill
What you ran it on. Worked, partly worked, or broke. Why, quoting the line that decided it.

## Agent
What you ran it on. Worked, went generic, or failed. What I needed from it and could not get. Name every file or folder it reached for that I don't have. Quote the line in its instructions that assumed my neighbour's own memory or files.

## What would have travelled
One of: the context, a skill, the output, a way to ask it. One line on why.

Save as handover-out.md and show it to me. I send it back; my neighbour saves it as module-7/handover.md.

Save the report as module-7/handover.md and read it together. The skill usually works on their system. It brings everything it needs. Your agent goes generic or fails, because it reads a memory your neighbour does not have. You gave them your agent, and it did not work for them. The skill did. Four things can travel: the context, a skill, the output, or a way to ask it. Which one you hand over is a strategy decision. The interview starts from module-7/handover.md.

Interview for the job

This is a heavy read across the working set. If the agent ranges too wide, interrupt with "tell me what you've found so far, narrow to the files that bear on this teammate, then continue." If it declares the job after a thin pass, say "there's more here. Keep reading before you settle the hypothesis."

Prompt (Claude Code Desktop)

Read module-7/handover.md first: what broke and what worked when my neighbour ran my skill and my agent on their system. Then read my memory/, sources/, module-3/, module-5/, and module-6/.

Based only on what you find there, draft a Jobs-to-be-Done hypothesis for a
sharing decision I'm working on. Cover four things:

1. The one teammate (named if my memory names them) most likely to benefit from
   what I've built.
2. The job they're trying to get done — in their language, not mine. Functional
   part, and at least one emotional or social part (anxiety, reputation,
   dependency on someone else).
3. Their current hire for this job — what they use today. Excel, a colleague,
   their gut, a vendor tool, nothing. Every job already has an incumbent.

Read module-7/jtbd.md. Does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe? If it could describe anyone in the room, point to the generic line and ask the agent to try that part again.

Pick against the outcome

The agent compares candidates from patterns/personal-to-team-patterns.md against that outcome and writes your choice to module-7/branch.md. The four sharing strategies:

  1. Share the context. Your memory/, sources/, root instructions, and style.md travel. Teammates' agents build on top.
  2. Share a skill. Extract one scoped capability. Teammates plug it in.
  3. Share the output (push). Schedule the agent. Output lands where the team looks.
  4. Share an interface (pull). Wrap the agent. Teammates invoke it through a bot, mention, form, or endpoint.

"Share the whole agent" is not on the list.

Read module-7/branch.md. Every picked candidate should name how it moves the teammate's outcome, with infrastructure only as a constraint. If the reason is "we already have the platform," send it back.

Carry the two files forward

Design the sharing plan finds what would stop that candidate from being absorbed and turns it into a technical plan plus a people plan.

Exercise

Exercise: Design the sharing plan

Time: 23 minutes.

module-7/jtbd.md names the job. module-7/branch.md names the candidate. Find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.

Find the absorption bottleneck

5 min

The obstacle is usually not the first technical limitation a builder sees. The agent compares the technical, social, political, habitual, governance, and trust obstacles and writes the load-bearing one.

Before it runs, look at your prework example: the tool people got and did not use. In one line, what stopped them?

Prompt (Cowork)

Find the absorption bottleneck in my sharing problem. Read module-7/jtbd.md and module-7/branch.md, plus anything else in module-7/ so far. The question is not "how do I share?" — it's "what's the single load-bearing obstacle between my teammate and firing their current hire?"

List the obstacles you see — technical, social, political, habitual, governance, trust. Cluster them. Name the bottleneck: the one that, if removed, makes several others easier. State it in one sentence.

Save to module-7/absorption-bottleneck.md. Show me before saving.

Draft both plans

18 min

The technical plan and people plan carry equal weight.

Prompt (Cowork)

Read module-7/jtbd.md, module-7/branch.md, and module-7/absorption-bottleneck.md. Draft two files in
parallel now — a technical plan and a people plan. Both are about whether this
teammate can actually fire their current hire and start using my candidate.

If either plan already exists, read it first and revise it in place. Preserve
supported detail; replace only what the current JTBD, branch, or bottleneck
evidence changes.

File 1: module-7/technical-plan.md — how the candidate delivers the outcome.
- What exactly I ship (files, skills, config, runtime).
- How the teammate receives it (zip, repo, connector, invite).
- What "it moves the outcome metric for them" looks like — concrete, measurable.
- The first real test case they'd run, against the job from the JTBD brief.

File 2: module-7/people-plan.md — equally load-bearing. Cover all five:
- Ownership: named person accountable. Not a role.
- Governance: who can add to the memory, change the rules, see the output.
- Operating: who notices when the outcome metric slips. What they do about it. If the obvious name is also the person who benefits most, name a second person who'd notice independently — otherwise the only alarm is the person with a reason to silence it.
- Accountability: who decides the candidate is no longer doing the job — who
  fires the hire.
- Propagation: who teaches the next person, when.

Ask only for a detail that blocks the draft. Don't invent names. If I don't know, write
"UNASSIGNED — Monday's question" and keep moving. Missing names are findings,
not failures.

Show me both before saving.

Take the transferable move with you

Before designing a solution, interview for the outcome. Pick the candidate against that outcome. Draft the technical and people plans together. Test the switch, not the solution. A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping. A candidate picked because it moves the outcome is design.

Lecture

Lecture: Access is not absorption

Access is easy; absorption is scarce

Many companies have rolled out access far ahead of trust. People can reach the agent. That does not mean they know when to use it, trust it with real work, or have a way to encounter it in the flow of the day.

Access is a switch somebody flips, and it completes in a minute. Absorption happens in other people's weeks, at their pace, for their reasons. The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.

The analysis was ready. The decision never came.

At the start of 2026 I set out to redesign a whole value stream with agents. We picked the slice that takes a company's flagship product to its millions of customers. Many teams touch it.

We built a multi-agent system for the work. About fifteen people across those teams mapped their own part and uploaded their own documents. A central agent pulled it all into one map of how the work flows today.

On the first workshop day, most of them refined that map together. People had fun, and bit by bit they learned how it works. On the second day a smaller group redesigned the flow. We left with a plausible proposal and the analysis to decide on it.

We had chosen this topic with the senior leadership before we started. By the decision meeting, the urgency had gone. New priorities had come up, and fires were burning elsewhere. The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.

The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had. Companies, even when they go agentic, work first and foremost on the human principle. Today, at least. Who knows about the future.

Antti Tevanlinna

Three parts copy, one does not

An agent is context, a boundary, a set of checks and somebody who answers for what it does. The first three copy in an afternoon. The fourth does not copy at all, which is why the product being sold as a shared agent is always three of the four parts, with the fourth still sitting with whoever built it.

Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.

Each strategy asks something different of the people receiving it

Share the context, and teammates have to trust your curation enough to build on it. Share a skill, and it has to fit into an agent they already run.

Share the output, and it has to appear where they already look, often enough to become a habit. Share an interface, and someone has to keep it running and answer for it when it is wrong.

Pick the one your teammate's week can take in.

The loop that ran while I was away

In November an agent of mine ran an eval loop for this course in the cloud. It simulated students and the judges that score them, until it hit my weekly limit. The cloud service scheduled it to resume when the limit reset.

The limit reset on a Friday evening. Two minutes later the loop started again. Nobody was at the keyboard.

It started about 33,000 sessions of its own. Nothing capped it. Nothing warned me. No usage counter showed any of it. Ten hours after the reset the week's quota was gone, and my other work stopped for the week.

Its message: "I'll continue then, so there's no need to do anything."

An agent running on a schedule still needs someone who answers for what it spends. That someone was me, and I was away.

Antti Tevanlinna

What would have to be true for them to switch?

Every job your teammate has already has a current solution: a spreadsheet, a colleague, a gut call that has worked well enough for years. Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.

So ask the question the other way round. Not how do I get them to adopt this? but what would have to be true for them to switch? The answers come back small and specific. It has to land where they already look. It has to be right the first time they try it. Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.

One name, one small move

You cannot schedule absorption from your side. It starts with one person and one conversation about how they do the job today.

module-7/monday.md holds that name, that question and the first test. Have the conversation before you build anything more. Their answer tells you which plan to keep.

Debrief

Who gets your context, who gets a skill, who wants only the output, and who would use an @mention? It is rarely the same person across all four.

Prompt (Cowork)

Start by identifying the file path. No plan or preamble.

Review this session and sharpen the sharing artifact. Read everything in module-7/ (jtbd, branch, absorption-bottleneck, technical-plan, people-plan, assumptions, failure-stories, monday) and identify which single file is the sharing artifact itself (the skill file, the interface spec, the output schedule, the context export, whichever pattern I picked produces the thing the teammate actually touches). Confirm the file path in one line before rewriting. Then look back over the session: where did the teammate's job-to-be-done stay unnamed or too abstract, where does the artifact leak more than the teammate needs (over-shared) or less than they can use (under-shared), where is the people plan thin (no name, no owner, no handoff), which assumption would have to be true for this to land and isn't? Be harsher than feels polite. If the people plan had no names, say so plainly.

Then rewrite the sharing artifact. Overwrite the file in place at its current path in module-7/; do not create a separate version. Integrate, don't append. Name the teammate's job explicitly at the top, tighten the surface area so it fits the job (not your whole system), add the one line the people plan needed. Keep the edge in the critique; the gap between people plan and real ownership is the message, not something to soften. Don't add a "retro notes" section; rewrite the file as the better version.

After the rewrite, when I push back on something specific, use Edit on the section I'm pushing back on, not Write on the whole file. Don't re-rewrite the whole artifact unless I say 'rewrite from scratch.'

When you're done, tell me in 3-5 lines: which file you rewrote, what you added, what you sharpened, what you removed, and why. For each claimed change, quote the before-and-after line or section header so I can confirm it landed. If you cannot quote the before-line, do not claim the change. Name the one assumption the artifact still depends on.

Then look back over the session: where did the teammate's job-to-be-done stay unnamed or too abstract, where does the artifact leak more than the teammate needs (over-shared) or less than they can use (under-shared), where is the people plan thin (no name, no owner, no handoff), which assumption would have to be true for this to land and isn't? Be harsher than feels polite. If the people plan had no names, say so plainly.

Then rewrite the sharing artifact. Overwrite the file in place at its current path in module-7/; do not create a separate version. Integrate, don't append. Name the teammate's job explicitly at the top, tighten the surface area so it fits the job (not your whole system), add the one line the people plan needed. Keep the edge in the critique; the gap between people plan and real ownership is the message, not something to soften. Don't add a "retro notes" section; rewrite the file as the better version.

After the rewrite, when I push back on something specific, use Edit on the section I'm pushing back on, not Write on the whole file. Don't re-rewrite the whole artifact unless I say 'rewrite from scratch.'

Key Concepts

  • Start with the teammate's job, not with what you built. Pick the candidate against that outcome. Infrastructure is a constraint, not a reason.
  • Share the context, a skill, the output (push) or an interface (pull). The handover showed which travels: the skill did, the agent without its memory did not.
  • The absorption bottleneck is the obstacle that keeps several others hard.
  • Write the technical plan and the people plan together.
  • Test what would have to be true for the teammate to switch.
  • Access is a switch someone flips. Absorption happens in other people's weeks.

Bring to Module 8

Bring module-7/monday.md, module-7/handover.md and what the named person said. Their answer is the evidence. The plan is still the hypothesis.

Next

You can build agents, secure them, evaluate them and share them four ways. What if an agent built the next one, for a gap someone else hit?

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Agents Building Agents (The Flywheel)

Big Idea

Agents building agents is how you and your organisation learn faster. Your agent can improve your agent, and from there a hundred agents is a matter of describing them.

Prework

Run module-7/monday.md: test one assumption, ask for one name, talk to one person, then have your agent write what they said into module-7/monday.md under ## What they said. Revisit three moves: find the crux, ask what would have to be true, run a pre-mortem.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Have agents build agents
  • Improve an agent with an agent
  • Write an agent strategy

Start here

Your agent works in ~/Documents/agents-101/ and reads your agent system plus module-7/monday.md and module-7/handover.md. The room's forum runs in a separate shared folder, so your own files stay local.

The shared folder starts nearly empty: one subfolder per participant, challenge.md from the buyer or sponsor, and one or two central synthesizers writing at the shared root.

The question to carry through: where is all this going?

Watch an agent build an agent

An agent can build agents. Describe the agent you want: the gap, what it reads, what it writes. It writes the instructions, runs the new agent, and fixes it when you push back.

It shares its parts with every agent it builds, so each one you describe makes the next one quicker.

Exercise

Exercise: Extend your system

Time: 25 minutes.

Session (new, "Module 8 - Agents building agents")

What you do:

In Module 7 your neighbour could not use your agent. Describe an agent for what they needed; an agent builds it, judges it and rebuilds it.

Phase 1: Describe the gap your neighbour hit

5 min

Open module-7/handover.md. It says what your neighbour needed and what broke without your files. Write four lines in module-8/extension-brief.md:

  • The gap: what your neighbour needed and could not get.
  • The job: what the agent does, on your neighbour's system.
  • What it reads: files your neighbour has. Nothing from your own folders.
  • What it writes: one named file.

Over five minutes? Narrow the gap.

Phase 2: An agent builds it

10 min

Prompt (Cowork)

Read module-8/extension-brief.md. Build the agent described in it. Choose a lowercase hyphenated filename from the job, not the technology. State the exact path under `agents/`, then draft the agent file at that path.

The agent file must include:
- Role (one sentence) — what job this agent is hired for
- Rules — carry forward the rules my existing agents follow (cite the memory file for every claim, never invent, ask when a source is thin). Add rules specific to this agent's job.
- Inputs — the exact files or folders this agent reads. Paths, not descriptions. For PDFs or slide exports, include an extraction-depth check and flag any file whose body text was not actually extracted.
- Output — the exact file or shape this agent writes. If it's a report, name the filename. If it's a response, describe the shape.
- Hard lines — things this agent must not do even if asked.

Show me the file before saving. After I approve, save it to the exact path you stated, then run it once end-to-end on real input from my system. Report what it produced, where it hesitated, and where a source was thin.

Phase 4: Hand it over

2 min

Send the built agent to your neighbour. Their agent runs it on their system.

Take stock of the compound

What happened:

In under half an hour an agent built an agent for a gap your colleague hit, and rebuilt it until the judge passed it.

The point:

Each agent you describe is built faster than the last. When agents build agents for each other's gaps, the organisation learns faster.

This is Recipe 8: agent generates agent, on a real gap. The Cookbook for Agent System Design holds the moves for the next gap, plus the rest of Recipe 8 for bigger moves than one agent.

Exercise

Exercise: Agent Proposal Forum, diagnose and guide

Time: 70 minutes, in nine timed stages.

What you do:

The buyer or sponsor seeds a live company challenge. The room's agents form a proposal forum around it: each takes a stance, cross-checks with the others, publishes proposals in the shared folder and criticizes the emerging selections. One or two central synthesizers keep choosing the best ideas.

The deliverable: your Rumelt-style strategy kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, near-term experiments, ranked risks), then a suggested agent set and execution plan.

The steps are the launch order. Agents keep reading and revising while later steps begin.

The six-line shape:

  1. Sponsor challenge: buyer or sponsor writes challenge.md at the shared root.
  2. Grounding: every agent writes context-manifest.md, listing what it carries and what it doesn't.
  3. Initial stance and cross-check: every agent writes stance.md, then reads neighbouring stances and writes cross-check.md.
  4. Shared proposals: every agent writes proposal.md; one or two central synthesizers publish selection-board.md.
  5. Critique loop: agents write critique.md with better ideas; the synthesizer updates selection-board.md.
  6. Conclusion: the synthesizer writes strategy-kernel.md, agent-set.md, and plan.md.

Phase 1: Ground the room

10 min

Each agent publishes what it has and what it doesn't have before another agent weighs its proposal. Every claim points at the file it came from.

Before you publish your context-manifest, redact customer names, partner-NDA material, M&A speculation and salary references. Other agents in the room read the manifest.

The trainer posts the shared folder path or name in chat at the start of Module 8. Use that exact folder for every shared-folder instruction. It is separate from your local training directory.

Prompt (buyer/sponsor agent, run once at the start)

Use the shared folder the trainer posted in chat. Write challenge.md at the shared folder root.

The challenge is:
"What should our company's strategy for agents be over the next six months?"

Make it concrete for this room:
- The buyer/sponsor goal in one paragraph.
- Three constraints the strategy must respect.
- Two non-negotiables.
- Three kinds of evidence that matter most.
- One decision the room must make today.

Do not solve it. Seed the challenge so the agents have something real to argue with.

Use the shared folder the trainer posted in chat. Write challenge.md at the shared folder root.

The challenge is:
"What should our company's strategy for agents be over the next six months?"

Make it concrete for this room:
- The buyer/sponsor goal in one paragraph.
- Three constraints the strategy must respect.
- Two non-negotiables.
- Three kinds of evidence that matter most.
- One decision the room must make today.

Do not solve it. Seed the challenge so the agents have something real to argue with.

- Which memory/ pages I have, by topic.
- Which sources/ I've fetched content for, vs. which are reference-only or NOT REACHABLE.
- Which custom agents I've built, by job.

Phase 2: Initial stance

8 min

Read the sponsor challenge and write your agent's opening stance. Don't read other stances yet: different context, sources and judgment make the first round useful. Your agent may ask you one or two clarifying questions first.

Prompt (Cowork)

Read challenge.md at the shared folder root.

Write my initial stance on the sponsor challenge.

Use Rumelt's crux move: name the load-bearing obstacle that, if removed, collapses several others. Then name the direction I currently favor.

Your ground is my own memory/, sources/, agents/, module-1/ through module-7/ outputs — including module-7/monday.md — plus module-8/built-agent.md, the agent I had built for a colleague's gap, plus my context-manifest.md so you know what I don't have. Do not read other participants' stance.md files yet. This first note should carry my agent's own position.

If you need human judgment before taking a stance, ask me up to two questions. After I answer, write the stance.

Rules:
- Every obstacle you name cites a file. "The sales team is skeptical" is not an obstacle — "sales-skepticism as described in module-3/interviews.md line 14" is.
- You must name at least one obstacle that lives outside your comfort zone — political, social, governance, trust — not only technical.
- Name the crux in one sentence.
- Name the direction I currently favor in one sentence.
- Name the human judgment call I am least certain about.
- Name one risk or objection my stance is weak against.

Save `stance.md` in the exact participant subfolder where you wrote `context-manifest.md`.

Phase 3: Cross-check with others

8 min

Once every stance.md is published, your agent reads three to five neighbouring stances, assigned by the trainer or the folders to your left and right. Find what your stance missed.

Prompt (Cowork)

Reuse the exact participant subfolder where you wrote `context-manifest.md`. Read its `stance.md`, then read three to five neighbouring `stance.md` files from other participant subfolders in the shared folder.

Write `cross-check.md` in that same subfolder with:
- One thing another agent saw that my stance missed.
- One disagreement I keep after reading the neighbours.
- One evidence gap that appears across more than one stance.
- One idea I should carry into my proposal.
- One stance I want the synthesizer to watch because it may be stronger than it first looks.

Do not summarize every neighbour. Act like a serious peer reviewer with skin in the game.

- Guiding policy, one sentence.
- Two experiments, each with owner, two-week test, success signal.
- What I changed after cross-checking with other agents.
- What I refused to change, and why.
- One unresolved disagreement the synthesizer must preserve.

Phase 5: Synthesizer starts choosing

8 min

The synthesizer reads proposals and chooses. With two, A picks the strongest ideas and B names objections, evidence gaps and unsafe assumptions. The sponsor pushes back; the synthesizer rewrites.

Central synthesizer prompt: "Read challenge.md and every participant subfolder in the shared folder from chat, using each stance.md, cross-check.md, and proposal.md. Do not average the room. Write selection-board.md at the shared folder root: best crux, guiding policy move, two-week experiment, objection, dangerous evidence gap, unresolved disagreement. Cite each source file and why it beats the alternatives. Mark it provisional."

Phase 6: Midway instruction injection

5 min

The central synthesizer publishes operating instructions in the shared folder. Your agents read them in the next step.

Prompt (central synthesizer)

Read selection-board.md at the shared folder root and every participant cross-check.md.

Write midway-instructions.md at the shared folder root with 3-5 operating instructions for the critique phase. These are not conclusions. They are rules for how agents should deliberate from here.

Include this instruction unless there is a stronger reason not to:
"Before criticizing the selection, cross-pollinate: read at least two participant folders whose proposals differ from yours, then carry forward one objection, one useful idea, and one evidence gap."

Also include instructions for:
- Which disagreement must not be averaged away.
- Which evidence gap must be named whenever it affects a claim.
- Which kind of claim needs a citation before the synthesizer can use it.
- Which tempting policy move should be treated skeptically.

Each instruction should be one sentence and usable by an agent that did not see the first round.

Phase 8: Final synthesis and the human decision

5 min

The central synthesizer reads every critique, updates the selection board, then writes the strategy kernel, the agent set and the plan. Any participant can publish a correction as pushback.md in their named subfolder; the synthesizer rewrites the conclusion.

The CTO, buyer or sponsor picks the two or three assumptions to test next. Without the sponsor, the room picks by show of hands and names the decision provisional.

Phase 9: Agent set, plan, and read-out

5 min

Close the session with three files at the shared folder root:

  • strategy-kernel.md
  • agent-set.md
  • plan.md

Write the strategy kernel's four sections

strategy-kernel.md has four sections:

  • Diagnosis. Selected crux and strongest rejected alternative, each citing its file.
  • Guiding policy. One-sentence policy move, Rumelt form.
  • Experiments. Two or three assumptions to test: owner, experiment, success signal.
  • Risks. Likeliest unseen pre-mortem failure; one early warning sign.

Prompt (central synthesizer)

Read challenge.md, selection-board.md, midway-instructions.md, every proposal.md, every critique.md, and any pushback.md files. Update selection-board.md if a critique changed the best idea.

Then write three files at the shared folder root:

1. strategy-kernel.md
Four sections: diagnosis, guiding policy, experiments, risks. Cite every claim against its source file. Keep the kernel under one page. Don't smooth the disagreements; where the selected idea beat a strong alternative, name the alternative in one line.

2. agent-set.md
Suggest the set of agents the company should build or assign next. For each agent: job, owner, input files/systems, output, first evaluation or judge, and why this agent belongs in the set. Keep it to the smallest set that can execute the plan.

3. plan.md
Write the plan for the next two weeks. Include sequence, owners, agent dependencies, human decision points, evidence to collect, success signal, and stop condition. Make clear which work can start concurrently and which work must wait.
